speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: U.S. ACTION RESPECTING ECONOMIC CREDITS TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Can the Prime Minister say
whether representations have been made by the United States to Canada and to other NATO nations in favour of denying the sale by any of those nations of unstrategic materials on a credit basis to the U.S.S.R.?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: U.S. ACTION RESPECTING ECONOMIC CREDITS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: I understand that reports have appeared in the press recently concerning discussions among NATO members on the subject of long term credit to the Soviet union and other communist countries in respect of the commodities which the right hon. gentleman has mentioned. As the house knows, it is the custom for members of NATO to hold periodic discussions relating to these and other matters of interest to the alliance. These discussions are, of course, of a confidential nature but I may say that no representations have been made to the Canadian government on this matter by the United States government or by any other government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: U.S. ACTION RESPECTING ECONOMIC CREDITS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister not agree that if such representations were made-and there have been many reports that they have been made to NATO countries other than Canada-Canada should take the same attitude as the United Kingdom and continue to sell on credit regardless of the wishes of the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: U.S. ACTION RESPECTING ECONOMIC CREDITS TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Since I have said no representations have been made, the right hon. gentleman's question is surely hypothetical.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. speechtext: I may state my privilege very succinctly and briefly. The Prime Minister says that orders of the day is not the time for us to ask these questions regarding federal-provincial relations. May I inform this house, as I reach my point of privilege, that before the month of June last year I asked a series of questions of the minister-

Mr. Speaker, if I could have silence I would state my question of privilege. Howling down by this arrogant government is something that cannot be condoned. Last June I asked at least two ministers pointed questions about federal-provincial relations. Subsequently I put on the order paper three motions for the production of papers asking for information. subtopic: OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS    PROVINCIAL WILLINGNESS TO SHARE IN INCREASE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS    PROVINCIAL WILLINGNESS TO SHARE IN INCREASE
speechtext: Hon. members may laugh, but it so happens that at this stage in Canadian confederation, federal-provincial relations are exercising the imaginations of many people. This is a new, subtle type of closure, when opposition members cannot get information.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS    PROVINCIAL WILLINGNESS TO SHARE IN INCREASE
speechtext:
Order. I have been as lenient as possible because, for obvious reasons, I was interested in hearing the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. It might be useful to recall to all hon. members citation 178 in Beau-chesne's fourth edition:
Questions addressed to ministers should relate to the public affairs with which they are officially connected, to proceedings pending in parliament, or to any matter of administration for which the minister is responsible. Within these lines an explanation can be sought regarding the intentions of the government, but not an expression of opinion upon matters of policy.
I do not believe the hon. member has anything more to add. At least the latter part of his statement I thought was out of order.

The question which comes to my mind is, why would a pipe line company rfnbark on the process of drilling and exploration unless it were going to embark on oil and gas production?
On November 9, 1962 the hon. member for Kingston, who since that time has been elevated another step in the hierarchy, had some very pointed things to say about special provisions being given to oil and gas companies. Quoting from page 1464 of Hansard for November 9, 1962 the hon. member for Kingston had this to say:
That is fine. Resolutions 6 to 10 primarily affect the oil and gas industry in Canada. It was estimated by the previous minister when they were introduced that they will cost the treasury some $15 million in a full year. The oil and gas industry as such will contribute very little to the income tax revenue of the federal government even though its gross revenue exceeds $500 million. I can think of no other industry in Canada in this favourable position.
It has been claimed that this industry needs further encouragement to find reserves. According to figures produced by the Canadian petroleum association, at the end of 1961 reserves on hand in Canada amounted to 18.9 years supply. If we compare our situation with the United States we will find that the United States had on hand at the same date some 12 years supply, and over the past 100 years the United States working inventory has ranged between 10 and 15 years-
What we need is more and faster growing markets for petroleum products. If we had these we would not need tax concessions to stimulate the search for oil. I suggest that the situation is no way changed from the time when the hon. member for Kingston made that very eloquent and telling speech, and I would urge the Minister of Finance, in view of his situation with regard to our national housekeeping, that he should cast a very dubious eye over this measure that he introduced some months ago, and determine whether this is justified in the light of Canada's present economic situation and in the light of his own views with regard to budgetary deficits. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands for complimenting iqe on my speech of last year, and I can assure him that my views generally toward these sections of the act have not changed. However, it was not deemed advisable to withdraw the sections in this particular budget, which was a decision of the government. In dealing with this particular clause, however, which is designed to extend the privileges which exist under the substance of the act to the pipe line companies, I am in complete agreement with it as such.
The majority of the independent pipe line companies in Canada are Canadian owned. As I recall it, three out of five are Canadian owned, and their position has been that they are not allowed the advantage of going out and developing their own raw materials to send through their own pipe lines. As these companies are to a large extent Canadian owned I would like to see them continue to exist, and they should have the same right as integrated companies to write off their exploration and development expenses. Integrated oil and pipe line companies can now write off their development expenses. The cost of going out and expanding their fields can be written off against the operations of their pipe lines, whereas an independent pipe line company cannot do this. In a similar sense you can take the large steel companies in Canada which have the

Income Tax Act
privilege of going out west and writing oil expenditures in this regard as against steel profits in eastern Canada.
The purpose of the section is to extend fair play to independent pipe line companies.

I find the hon. member's argument singularly unpersuasive. What he is telling us is that we are allowing some people unjustifiably to get into the public treasury and we should allow others to exercise their sticky fingers in the same way. Any pipe line company that embarks on a program of development and exploration becomes an integrated company. It has an integrated operation. At any rate, I suggest that last year the hon. member for Kingston considered these allowances to be scandalously unjustified; and to give them to other companies just because some companies have these allowances, which he considers scandalously unjustified, does not seem to me a suitable argument for extending the scandal a little farther even under the guise of these other companies being true blue Canadian companies.
I do not think it really matters very much to the Canadian consumer whether he is robbed by a Canadian or robbed by a foreigner. On the other hand, I do suggest this is something that indicates the necessity for a complete overhaul of this section of our fiscal set-up, and I would be much better pleased to see the minister come forward with a completely revamped structure in this regard rather than, as I say, compounding the mistake that has already been made in regard to existing companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If I may, I should like to make my position clear. Last year I was against all these allowances and the sections in the act dealing with them. Quite honestly I still have grave doubts with regard to their validity from a taxation point of view. Let me first state that. However, since it has been the decision of the government to allow these sections to stand, I think there is a strong argument that the same benefits should be extended to the independent pipe line companies as are extended to the large integrated companies at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I have been interested in this hybrid section of the Income Tax Act for a good many years. I want to support what the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has said. I cannot continue without complimenting him on his elephantine memory, which is very useful on occasions.
[Mr. Benson.)
We object to this type of legislation regardless of the explanation, and one could see that the parliamentary secretary was most uncomfortable in having to make a retreat on account of expediency. We object in principle to this type of legislation which permits these corporations to deduct from their taxable income the cost of mining operations and in other cases the cost of well drilling and pipe lines. As a matter of fact, on account of this legislation being in the Income Tax Act the Canadian people have financed United States subsidiaries in Canada to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars. Then we are told we have not got the capital in Canada.
I want to take the opportunity to mention again something I have mentioned in previous years, because it is obvious that the government is going to continue this same practice on this occasion. We have been told repeatedly that this type of clause in the Income Tax Act was intended to promote investment and increase production in Canada. That is what we were told some years ago when it was first introduced into the Income Tax Act.
I want to ask the minister this question. On the basis of that argument, and if the principle is going to be continued, has any further consideration been given to extending the same advantages to farmers who increase production as a result of clearing, draining or irrigating land? All these activities increase production. The farmer, who is a small person compared to these companies, gets no advantage at the present time although he does exactly the same thing that these large companies which are taking advantage of the act are doing.
I also want to bring to the attention of the minister a paragraph in the annual report of the Department of Forestry for 1961-62. Under the heading "Study of the Effects of Income Tax on Private Timber Management" it reads as follows:
This study was begun in co-operation with officials of the taxation divisions of the Departments of Finance and National Revenue in response to representations that have been made to the government. Its purpose is to examine the merits of recommended tax changes that would modify the taxing of income that is solely attributable to timber growth. The study should reveal conditions under which the growing of timber by private enterprise will be encouraged.
I want to ask the minister two questions before I sit down. First, has consideration been given to extending to the farmers of the country who increase production by any method the same privileges that are extended to these large corporations? Second, what has been the result of the study referred to in this report, and is the department giving consideration to extending the same privileges

Income Tax Act
to tree farmers who are farming on management principles over a long term and who are increasing production while at the same time, because of their practices, maintaining a perpetual yield and conserving our forest resource capital in so far as that comes within their jurisdiction? Is the minister giving any consideration to amending the act in the future to allow these people to enjoy the same privileges as large corporations?

On clause 22-Tax.

I have an amendment to propose to clause 22 to which I invite the attention of the committee. I shall move the same amendment to clauses 23 and 28 when they are reached.
Clause 22 imposes a special tax of 5 per cent on certain dividends and corporations which do not have "a degree of Canadian ownership and control". I invite the committee to notice the words "and control". I might mention for the sake of completeness that clause 23 uses the same phrase. It alters the rate of the withholding tax so as to impose a tax of 10 per cent after the date fixed in the clause dealing with dividend payments by corporations with "a degree of Canadian ownership and control"; it imposes a 20 per cent withholding tax on corporations which do not so qualify.
Clause 28 defines what is to be deemed, for the purposes of the act-that is covered by clauses 22 and 23-a corporation which has a degree of Canadian ownership and control. By clause 28 a corporation is deemed to have a degree of Canadian ownership and control if two alternative conditions and another condition exist; that is to say, if 25 per cent of the voting shares are owned in Canada; second, if shares are listed on a Canadian exchange and no one foreign shareholder owns more than 75 per cent of the stock; and third, there is another condition that not less than 25 per cent of the directors are resident in Canada.
My proposed amendment will strike out of the phrase "a degree of Canadian ownership and control" wherever it appears the words "and control". The effect of the amendment would not be to change the substantive tax; the tax will remain precisely the same. The purpose of the amendment is to remove from the act what might be called a false and misleading label or description.
It is not necessary for me to discuss the merits of the proposed change. At the resolution stage we expressed our reasons for feeling that the proposed change did not achieve the stated purpose of encouraging Canadian control of industry, but in fact discouraged it. We in this party are all in

favour of effective legislation to encourage Canadian control of Canadian industry, but in my submission the label put on these corporations, which would benefit from the proposed incentives, of "a degree of Canadian ownership and control" is false and misleading. The words "and control" are meaningless. Under this definition a corporation can qualify for the incentives which could not, by any fair stretch of the language, be said to have a single trace of Canadian control. For example, a 25 per cent interest may in certain cases give a measure of control, but in the case of a wholly owned United States subsidiary, which is the most typical case with which we are dealing here, there would be no element of control whatsoever.
The same reasoning applies even more clearly to that part of the clause which states that all that is required to qualify is that shares should be listed on an exchange, and that no one foreign shareholder should own more than 75 per cent of the stock. Nor does the provision that one out of four directors should be resident in Canada give any measure or degree of Canadian control. It would be perfectly easy to have what is known as a dummy director, who to all intents and purposes would actually be 100 per cent subservient to the foreign shareholders. If I as a lawyer, or any other learned hon. member, were asked to give advice as to whether in the case of a corporation with 25 per cent of the shares owned in Canada and with one dummy director resident in Canada it could be said that there was any degree of control over that company, I would be negligent if I said yes. I would be fired from my job if were to be so misleading as to suggest that that state of affairs constituted any degree of control. There is no such thing as a degree of control; there is either control or no control. This state of affairs represents no control whatever.
My objection to the wording of the clause is not a frivolous or pedantic one. People are prosecuted who attach false labels to goods and then seek to sell them to the public, and they are rightly prosecuted. We condemn, and properly so, false advertising. Yet the government of Canada can sell this legislation to the public on the pretext that it is giving incentives and encouraging Canadian control over Canadian industry. This claim is not true. In my view parliament should set an example of honesty. According to the legal authorities it is true that parliament can declare black to be white and white to be black. I believe it was the famous Sir Edward Coke who said that.
But notwithstanding our right to declare white to be black and black to be white,

we must not be misleading. It is my view that it is misleading to define a corporation, lor purposes ol tax incentives, as having a degree of Canadian ownership and control when there may well be not one iota or scintilla of Canadian control involved. Therefore I move:
That clause 22 of the bill be amended by striking out from subsection (1) (a) and (1) (b) thereof the words "and control".
If this amendment meets with the approval of the committee I will move a similar amendment in respect of clause 23, where the words appear, and clause 28 when the same phrase appears.

I think this may well come as a surprise to the minister, but so far as clause 22 is concerned, which is section 105B (a), there is a complete divergence of expression. What is said in the French version is not what is said in the English version. The English version says:
-did not have a degree of Canadian ownership and control.
The French version says:
-n'etait dans aucune mesure possidie oil con-tr6l6e.
When we turn to clause 28, which is the definition clause, the meaning is the same in French as in English. Therefore there will have to be a necessary amendment to the French version to bring it in line with the thinking expressed by the act.
Having said that with respect to the drafting, I must say that I would go even further than the hon. member for Greenwood and repeat the remarks I made on the resolution stage and on second reading, that so far as the Canadianization or the patriation of capital is concerned, this provision means precisely nothing. It is already simple to have foreigners or non-Canadian citizens resident in Canada hold office for a period as managers or as local officials of companies. I refer particularly to smaller companies, not the larger ones; the privately held and controlled companies. I do not know many subsidiary companies in Canada which are public companies; they are primarily wholly owned or closely controlled subsidiaries of foreign corporations. To say that you are going to have a greater degree of control because you have Canadian residents or residents of Canada as directors is frankly nonsense. If you are going to have Canadian ownership and control, then these people must ba Canadian citizens.
I realize the minister may say that this is introducing into the act a concept of nationality or citizenship which does not exist in other parts of the Income Tax Act. There
Income Tax Act
is nothing else in the act which offers incentives to companies which have a Canadian nature, and the Canadian nature comes about by reason of this so-called ownership or control. The minister is himself introducing an exception into the act in this regard by providing for these incentives.
If he is trying to patriate foreign capital, let him go all the way. He is offering an incentive to capital. All right; let us make it Canadian. I cannot see the logic of the argument that because this provision does not exist elsewhere in the act it must not be introduced now; that we must not allow the principle of citizenship but, rather, that we must look merely to residence. I find the whole provision in this connection to be meaningless.
With regard to the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Greenwood, I think there may be some justification for it, though the words "and control" seem to be a reference to the directors rather than to the so-called ownership. It comes down to this. The hon. member is asking us to delete or subtract something from nothing.

Does the minister wish to comment or make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have made several statements on this subject. If the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has anything to say about it I am sure we would be happy to hear from him, but I am not sure whether this other matter ought not to be disposed of first.

I think we would wish to take a look at the proposed amendment. I assume the minister is not urging that there should be a division on this at once. I should

like to look at it and see what effect the proposal might have. There is no point in having a vote on it right now, particularly in view of the ruling of the Chair that it must be applicable to a certain specific clause. I think we should study the application of the proposed amendment to the various clauses, and when we have done so we shall be in a better position to reach an opinion with regard to it.
I do not intend to speak at any length on this part of the bill. As the minister has just indicated, we have discussed the matter at some length on other occasions. I spoke on it, as did other hon. members, during the resolution stage. We spoke on it again on second reading and now we are in committee. I do not propose to reiterate arguments which have already been advanced, or to weary the committee by repetition.
However, speaking for members on this side, for the official opposition at least, let me say I feel this clause introduces a new principle into the taxation law, a principle which in my view is of very dubious merit and which may do tremendous damage to the Canadian economy. We cannot allow the clause to pass in silence, contenting ourselves with the reflection that since we spoke about it before we need not say anything about it now.
I think no one would quarrel with the minister's motivation, his desire to have a greater degree of ownership by Canadians in corporations in Canada. We should all like to see a greater degree of Canadian ownership of our corporate structure. We in Canada, of course, are in a different position from the United States where corporations were established many, many years ago before the incidence of income tax and succession duties, when there was a tremendous pool of capital in Britain to be used for the development of the United States through the purchase of bonds and fixed income securities. The holders clipped the coupons and paid no income tax on the dividends. Finally United States corporations paid up the bonds and secured ownership of the equities.
That could not be done today because of the incidence of taxation. Investors generally are looking forward to capital appreciation; they are interested in equity holdings rather than the collection of dividends. The result is ownership rather than the holding of money, and this is the way in which our corporate structure in Canada differs from that of the United States.
I accept the theory that it is desirable to have ownership in Canada. On the other hand, I do not necessarily accept the argument that ownership by outside interests of Canadian

corporations or of corporations in Canada means there can be any great degree of political control of Canada or of Canadian institutions. I do not think this has been proven, and I doubt if it can be proven. There is, of course, a tremendous degree of foreign ownership. The minister has given us the figures of foreign ownership, mainly United States ownership, of our corporate structure. I am sure all of us who have had some experience with government know that from time to time problems arise in this connection. There are, perhaps, statutes in other countries which do tend to have an impact upon corporations outside the nation, but I have never seen them amount to any degree of interference with the Canadian political organization or with the government of Canada per se.
I do not believe it has existed. I do not believe it will exist, and I do not accept the argument that because a certain percentage of our corporate structure is owned by another country there is great danger of losing political control over our own institutions. I do not think we face this menace which is sometimes conjured up in week end magazines and newspaper headlines.
I noticed last week in Newsweek magazine -I do not suggest that this periodical has biblical authority, but it is sometimes quoted as being worthy of attention-an article referring to the degree of independence now being exercised by various countries which we used to call satellites of Russia-Rumania, Poland, and the rest-despite not only economic control but political control. The article, whether it is right or wrong suggested there was a fairly high degree of independence being exercised by those countries. If that is true, then it is rather fallacious to suggest we are going to lose control of this country because there are corporations in New York or Detroit which have ownership of our corporations.
Canada certainly would be a far different country if we did not have this United States control. We may not like it; we may not like to have the effects of it, but I wonder how much employment there would be in Canada today if we did not have this degree of United States ownership and control. I know in my own constituency, which is a rural constituency, there have been three corporations come in within the last 18 months. They are wholly owned subsidiaries of United States corporations employing several hundred people. Certainly they have integrated into the local economy, into the society of the community, and are becoming remarkably good citizens. The same situation applies all over Canada.
28902-5-290
Income Tax Act
As I have said, we can have some sympathy for the minister in his desire, a laudable desire. If we were rewriting the history of the world or reconstituting this nation, things might be done differently. I do not believe this provision is as essential as the minister urges. However, that is not my worry. If it is not as essential, and I suggest it is not, then I can see where very real difficulties might arise from the implementation of these measures which are put forward in this legislation. Great difficulties might be created for this country in the future.
As I said, what is the future going to be in respect of Canadian subsidiaries in the United States? After I sit down I should like the minister to discuss with us the situation in relation to the United States-Canada tax convention. We have conventions, of course, as hon. members know with various countries such as the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Germany. I could run through a long list of them. As I recall it, and I am subject to correction, there is only one of these conventions under which a provision can be abrogated immediately, and that is the Canada-United States convention. This convention provides that if one country takes action to increase the tax beyond the 15 per cent, then automatically that section has been abrogated. In every other case, the United Kingdom, Belgium, and so on, as I recall it you would have to give notice before the first day of June in one year and the notice of abrogation would become effective on December 31 of the next succeeding year. In this case, once we pass this bill which the minister has before us providing for an increase in the withholding tax from 15 per cent to 20 per cent, the Canada-United States convention is abrogated.
It may be argued, and no doubt this is the hope of the minister, that since this provision does not become effective until next year it will not be construed as an abrogation, that there will be lots of time to renegotiate the treaty; after all, this is only November and we have December, January and a few more months in which things can be done; that we can renegotiate the treaty in the meantime. 1 am sure the minister has had discussions on this matter with the authorities in Washington, and perhaps has received assurance as to what they hope can be done. Nevertheless I am suggesting that once His Excellency gives approval to this bill, then technically we have abrogated the convention. Although the measure does not become effective until next year, our friends in the United States could consider the passage of the measure

Income Tax Act
now an abrogation of the convention. In any event, it is said, we have from now until 1964.
How long does it take to renegotiate a convention? I can tell the minister, I am sure the minister has been told, and if he has not his colleague the Minister of National Revenue could remind him very forcibly of what happened in the department not too long ago when this parliament changed from a succession to an estates tax act. This was merely a technical change. There were some changes in the rates, but there were no provisions in the bill applying to any one country. There was no resentment created. This was a simple matter for the Canadian parliament to decide, yet what happened? Immediately after the act was passed and the usual claims were going back and forth relating to the taxation of estates on the United States side, the United States said the treaty was broken. We had a succession duty act and now we have an estates tax act. It does not apply; we have to renegotiate the treaty. It was very simple; there were no problems. However, in spite of this, as I recall it took over two years to renegotiate this simple treaty. There was not so much time spent in the negotiation of it, because all that can be done by officials in a few hours, and it was.
We must not forget, however, that any treaty has to be enacted by the Senate of the United States. The Senate is a sovereign parliamentary body such as this. It does not intend to be pushed into the passage of an enactment, with the heavy calendar that it has. I am wondering just how long it is going to be or what the minister proposes in relation to the renegotiation of the treaty. If I understand the law in this regard-I may be wrong but I do not think I am-once this treaty is abrogated we are going to have a 30 per cent withholding tax. This is the United States taxation law, once a tax convention is abrogated. We have a good many Canadian corporations in the United States, perhaps not as many as we would like but I think Canadians are apt to overlook this. There are a number of Canadian corporations doing business in the United States. I have not had time to prepare a study of this, but if one reads the returns of the Department of National Revenue under tax schedule 1, or reads the report of the Bank of Canada, one will be pleasantly surprised to find the degree of ownership by Canadians of corporations in the United States.
I suggest, and I think the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Trade and Commerce would not quarrel with the argument, that this is one way we can develop our trade, by having subsidiaries in other countries and particularly in the United

States. They are doing this. We can think of the Moore Corporation and probably a dozen others. If these corporations are going to be subject to a 30 per cent withholding tax, what is going to be the result? Obviously there is going to be a change, and a field day for corporation lawyers. I should like to exchange the seat I have now for a partnership in some firm in Toronto. Obviously the corporate structure will have to be reorganized in these Canadian corporations; at least this is a possibility, and I think more than a possibility. They will become holding companies, and the Canadian parent will become the subsidiary. The whole corporate structure of these companies will be changed very drastically. We may well end up with United States corporations paying taxes to the United States government, and we will have branches of what were once Canadian parent corporations.
This is one problem that could arise out of this bill. The minister may be able to clarify the situation this afternoon as we proceed with the discussion. As I have said, in my opinion this is one of the most important legislative measures to come before parliament, with all due respect to the very important matters we have discussed during the week. I believe that every section of an income tax bill or any taxation bill is important to individuals, sometimes to scores and sometimes to thousands. This, I think, is important to the nation as a whole, and is something to which we in this parliament should give very careful consideration.
The minister has said it is the intention of the government to pass this measure. I am not proposing to move any technical amendments to it at the moment. The purpose of the measure is to obtain a greater degree of ownership of corporations here in this country. Suppose you have United States subsidiaries here, and there are hundreds of them; and suppose that, rightly or wrongly, they believe this law may be changed some day, that it is unworkable. If they are paying dividends they could stop the payment of dividends for the time being, and what would have been paid in dividends to people in the United States, on which the corporation would have to pay this 20 per cent, would be transferred to capital reserve, and that money would be used for expansion in Canada. So there would be a greater concentration of American ownership in Canada because we were penalizing them for sending the money out, and they would use the money for expanding here in Canada. The last state would be worse than the first. What the minister is trying to avoid could easily become the reverse because of the situation I have mentioned.

I said I did not intend to speak at length on this matter, but I have developed a little further some of the general arguments I advanced previously. We feel very strongly that this is a matter to which parliament should give a great deal of attention. Giving the minister full credit for his laudable desire to develop a national spirit, and so on, we feel this is the wrong way, and that we are starting off in a tax situation where we are penalizing one class as against another.
We have discrimination for the first time, and the minister has replied that this has happened before. I am not going into a corporate debate on it; but after the minister said that, I had representations made to me that if in fact discrimination may have taken place previously it was done by corporation statutes rather than through taxation statutes. I am doubtful if there is any other tax statute in the western world, certainly not in the British commonwealth, where you get discrimination between two classes of taxpayers, as is proposed to be set up through this bill. I think it is a wrong principle and one-

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes, but I cannot guarantee to answer it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He has made reference to the fact that there are no tax statutes in other countries which control foreign investments in this way and that the same purpose was achieved by corporation statutes. Can he refer to any other country which has the same division of legislative jurisdiction that we have? Is he not aware that this is a constitutional problem?

It may very well be a constitutional problem, but we are dealing here with a tax statute and we have always applied equality of taxation. I suggest that we are departing from this principle in the bill that we have before us at the moment.
I am sure there are others of my colleagues on this side of the house who will want to discuss this matter, but I am particularly interested in hearing what the minister has to say about tax conventions and the possibility of renegotiating them. I do not have to remind the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce of the negotiations which this country will have to carry on in GATT. As the Prime Minister once said, there are and will be no easy or automatic solutions to our problems in the future. They are becoming more closely interwoven and interlocked with the trading problems of other nations.

Income Tax Act
Already we have a document which has appeared in the United States press, and rightly or wrongly the United States resents this type of legislation. The United States press thinks it is anti-American. At any rate it is technically, because that is the only country in the world with which we have a tax convention which is automatically abrogated when we approve of this tax. We have to give notice to every other country, but technically at least this is anti-American, and it is creating a substantial degree of resentment in certain quarters in the United States.
We need United States capital coming into this country, and we need co-operation in our international negotiations which will be conducted this year, next year, and I suppose on into eternity, because they have become part of our permanent way of life. One should be very careful in bringing forward legislation such as this even for a laudable but sort of will o' the wisp-with all due respect-intention that the minister has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will try and answer some of the points raised by the hon. member. In the first place, so far as I could gather, he raised some very grave doubts about doing anything in this general area of trying to get a greater degree of control of the Canadian economy back into Canadian hands. He raised a number of bogies and a number of points which were raised previously and which we have tried to answer previously.
The one with the most substance was that if we do anything like this we will annoy people, and therefore we will not be able to get the capital we need in the future. I would remind the hon. gentleman that the most important part of this bill-it is not this clause but I hope I will be allowed to refer to it because it has a bearing on it-in some ways the most important part of this bill is that which relieves certain institutions in other countries from a withholding tax on bond interest that they receive, provided those institutions do not pay tax in their own country.
There has been very little said on this point, and perhaps I am at fault because I have not emphasized it. However, I do so in relation to this clause because it has a bearing on it. This means that with the passing of that particular clause, and with the exemption of withholding tax on this particular kind of interest, we will open up an opportunity in this country to sell securities to one of the fastest growing accumulations of capital funds that exists. These pension funds by and large would not touch Canadian bonds since the withholding tax of 15 per cent was imposed on bond interest in the budget of December, 1960. That action eliminated this very large capital pool from Canadian borrowers, and in

Income Tax Act
addition that 15 per cent tax on bond interest payable to non-residents has increased the cost of money in Canada.
It is a firm part of this government's economic policy that we should keep interest charges as low as possible, having regard to the rates of interest charged in other countries. Therefore I suggest to the hon. member that this fear of his in relation to this withholding tax on dividends should be related, at least to some extent, to the other measures that are proposed in this bill, which to me, in so far as future capital requirements are concerned, are far more important.

I do not want to interrupt the minister, but does he have any other instances? Has he any other clauses similar to that which he wants to draw to the attention of the committee, or is that the principal one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I mean to get back to this clause.
This is the principal one to which the minister refers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, for now. The hon. member in his recitation of the facts that troubled him about this particular clause raised the question of the tax treaties and the fact that they will have to be renegotiated. Well, that is true; quite apart from the tax treaty with the United States, our tax treaties with all other countries have to be renegotiated because of the changes in the withholding taxes imposed in December, 1960.
Apart from the one with the United States, in the case of all others notice must be given before the end of June. Notice was not given before the end of June 1961. Notice was not given before the end of June 1962. When I became Minister of Finance last April one of the questions that was raised with me, and to which I gave considerable attention, was whether in June 1963 we should give notice to all these other countries that we intended to renegotiate our tax treaties with them, as we must do. I thought at that time it would be better to wait until this bill had been passed before giving that notice. It is perfectly obvious however this is something that has been hanging fire for three years, and that it must be attended to in the very near future.
I think, Mr. Chairman, I said all the treaties have to be renegotiated. There are one or two which do not, but certainly the majority of them have to be renegotiated. In the meantime-and I do not think this has been fully appreciated-the recipients of dividends from Canada in quite a number of countries have been getting their dividends tax, despite the fact that the law provides for a 15 per cent withholding tax, and has done so ever

since December 1960. They have got this income free of tax because these treaties have not been renegotiated.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that it is high time we attended to that particular piece of business, and I can assure him we propose to do so as soon as this bill is passed. As to the tax treaty with the United States, there is a provision in it that as soon as a higher rate than 15 per cent is imposed, then under United States law their withholding tax goes to 30 per cent.
As the hon. member suggested, we have had some preliminary conversations about this matter. As I said the other day, it was suggested to us that, first, these proposed changes in the withholding taxes do not become effective until January, 1965 and so, if I remember the words correctly, it was suggested that there was no immediate hurry. Second, it was suggested to us that it would be preferable from the standpoint of the officials who will be doing the renegotiation on the American side to wait until the bill had been passed. They asked me when the bill would be passed and I said, perhaps rather optimistically, that I hoped it would be passed by the middle of October. But things move slowly.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is my out because I did not mention any year. I might say I do not expect to be confronted with quite the arbitrary approach that I think the hon. member perhaps had in mind. After all, when this matter is examined, naturally we will point out that the withholding taxes are being reduced from 15 to 10 per cent in a number of cases, not increased, and that they are being increased from 15 to 20 per cent in a number of others but not effective until 1965. It is anybody's guess as to how these things will balance out exactly, but my officials are inclined to think that we will be collecting a little less rather than more in the way of withholding taxes on these dividends.
I think also that most people know that the amount of United States investment in Canada very greatly exceeds the amount of Canadian investment in the United States, and I daresay this point will not be overlooked in the negotiations. Certainly we will point it out. The hon. member was worried about certain Canadian companies that have subsidiaries in the United States. I have no doubt he had in mind Distillers Corporation, Hiram Walker and Gooderham and Worts.
We have never heard of them down in the valley.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member is not interested in the products of these companies. I am sorry about that; possibly I can change his mind after this committee rises. But these companies naturally have been making representations, as they are nervous about the matter; and I can assure them and also the hon. member that we will be keeping their problems very much in mind. I am not quite as convinced as he seemed to be that it is so simple just to move out of Canada arid establish a head office in the United States. There are some technical problems about which his predecessor, who is now a leading counsel with a Toronto firm, might be able to inform him if the hon. member needs that information.
I am looking forward to it.

speechtext:
Perhaps I could call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee rose at one o'clock we were considering clause 22. Shall clause 22 carry?
Mr. Chairman, there was an amendment which the minister proposed to put forward, I think, or if not, 1 do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are in fact two amendments to this clause, Mr. Chairman. During the luncheon recess we had some discussion about this matter, and before we get on to the particular amendment perhaps I might be permitted to finish the remarks I was making in reply to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
One of the points made by the hon. member was that he said he knew of no other instance where the taxing statutes were used in a way which was discriminatory, and that we and other countries have always used these tax statutes in such a way that taxes were applied equally. With the greatest respect I suggest to him that this may be true, but depending on the narrowness or breadth of the interpretation used. I remind him, to take a rather narrow example, that it was not very long ago that there were differences in the rates of withholding tax. The rate was 5 per cent in the case of dividends paid by subsidiaries substantially owned by corporations in other countries. The rate was greater in the case of dividends paid by other companies where there was not a very high degree of control. Certainly that form of discrimination existed, and I personally think that it was pointed in the wrong direction. I said that on many occasions to several
Income Tax Act
previous governments. There certainly was a differential in the rates and to that extent there was discrimination.
Following up the point raised this morning by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, he said that certain industries in this country have for many years received incentives or a form of reduced taxation which did not apply to other industries. I think the hon.' member suggested this gave the oil companies certain advantages. I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam suggested that this was one of the reasons why the oil industry in Canada is pretty well dominated by foreign concerns. I am not going into the reasons why this form of incentive was given. I do not even propose to discuss whether, in the end result, it was not quite useful, because it did result in the development of our oil industry. I mention it because the companies which received most of the benefit were relatively few in number, and they were controlled in other countries.
I suggest this could be interpreted as a form of discrimination in their favour. I mention it only because to me all taxation is bound to be discriminatory. Parliament decides on the rates, and in their wisdom successive parliaments have decided to charge different rates in the case of individuals, depending on the amount of their total incomes. I do not suppose there are many hon. members of the committee who do not believe that a progressive rate of taxation as far as personal incomes are concerned is a reasonable way to redistribute income and to some extent redistribute wealth. In any event the progressive personal income tax is established in this country and I doubt very much that it will be abandoned in the near future.
I could give a number of examples to show that by and large there are many forms of discrimination in the tax statutes; I suppose it is inherent in the method of collecting government revenues, and always has been. Someone might ask why in this enlightened age we still collect customs duties. Other people may think, as I am sure some of my hon. friends opposite do, that we would be better off if there was no personal income tax. I do not think the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands would share that point of view, but others might.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: When the minister refers to friends opposite, I think he should indicate what part of the house he has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should be so sensitive. Any reader of Hansard would be able to tell from the context of my remarks which particular friends I was referring to

Income Tax Act
at a given moment. I am glad to say I have friends in all parts of the house; at least I hope so.
I do not think this issue should be interpreted as dogmatically as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings did this morning. The question has been asked why it was necessary to increase to 20 per cent the rate of non-resident withholding tax on dividends paid by companies which do not have a degree of Canadian ownership and control. That was the phrase originally used. I should perhaps now say "foreign ownership" in deference to the hon. member for Greenwood. The government desired to provide a worth while inducement for non-residents to release ownership of some shares in those subsidiaries in Canada in which there is now little or no Canadian participation. Since the non-resident withholding tax falls directly upon the nonresident who owns shares in Canadian companies, it is the tax which can best be used to encourage non-residents to make way for a reasonable degree of Canadian ownership.
To be effective, a tax inducement of this kind must amount to more than a few percentage points. Accordingly it is proposed that a relatively low rate of 10 per cent be provided where dividends are paid by companies with a degree of Canadian ownership, and that a rate of 20 per cent, which is more than can be absorbed by foreign tax credits in most cases, be imposed after a reasonable period in those cases where the paying company has not acquired a degree of Canadian ownership.
I do not think it would be particularly profitable for me to review at this point what I have said on other occasions about this clause. The fact is that this is, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said, if I recall his words correctly, a timid first step in the right direction. I am not prepared, in view of what has happened in the last few months, to admit it is as timid a step as the hon. member has suggested, but I am prepared to say it is a first step and I would hope all members of the committee would support it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What about the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been proposed, Mr. Chairman, that instead of amending each of several clauses there be one amendment at the end which would deal with all the clauses and which would refer specifically to them and to the lines in the bill where the changes should be made. The amendment could be moved now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I think that would be better. Otherwise we would have passed the clause and we would have to reopen it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I so move.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there is another amendment which the Minister of Public Works would like to move. It applies to the clause we are now considering. Between the resolution stage and the drafting of the bill certain words which were in parenthesis were omitted. They should be reinstated. The amendment reads:
That Bill C-95, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, be amended by striking out line 17 on page 18 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
"corporation (other than a non-resident-owned investment corporation) as, on account or in lieu of payment"

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I so move.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Before the clause as amended is carried, I should like to say a few words concerning this part of the bill. The minister indicated a moment ago that these provisions represented at least a first step. I suggest it is a first step down the wrong path. It occurs to me that the minister is approaching this problem in an altogether incorrect way. I appreciate that there is a problem. I under-we are now considering. Between the resolu-stand what the hon. gentleman is trying to do. My hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings, when he spoke before the recess, also said he appreciated the problem which the minister faces. We all do; but surely this is the wrong way to go about remedying it.
I think this is a retrograde step. I think it will be found unworkable, and in the few minutes during which I intend to speak I shall try to point out the inconsistencies

which it appears to me to contain. I believe this legislation is iniquitous and discriminatory. I suggest that an entirely different approach should be taken. Instead of penalizing people who wish to invest money in Canada, encouragement should be given to Canadian citizens to invest in their own equity securities. A more positive approach should be taken. The minister said this was a small step. I think it is a huge step in our relationship with other countries. I think the whole question should have been set aside until a report had been received from the royal commission on taxation.
The minister said my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings had indicated that this provision would annoy people. Then the minister commented that whatever kind of tax might be imposed, some people would be annoyed. It is true that everybody is annoyed when a tax which they have to pay goes up by 1 per cent, or when some move such as this is made. But this particular provision does seem to me to be going off the wrong end. I agree with the statement made in the Globe and Mail of October 21, that this does appear to be an egghead approach.
My hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings said there were three subsidiaries of United States companies in his riding. I could name innumerable companies of this kind. I was talking to a representative of one the other day. His company had a lengthy lease. It did not expire for another year, and they had been about to exercise their option to purchase. Well, they are now reconsidering the whole move. The expression used to me in this connection was "Why should we do this when there appears to be a climate in which we are not wanted?" The financial climate in Canada today is such as to discourage foreign capital from entering Canada, and to discourage the holding of capital in Canada.
Even if the steps which are now proposed were in fact taken, what would be the result? What would happen if a company were to sell 25 per cent of its interest in Canada in order to take advantage of the 10 per cent differential in the withholding tax? What would happen to the amount for which they had sold the interest? Undoubtedly the parent company would take it out of the country, to the United States or whatever country was concerned. If they were going to sell any share of the corporation they would undoubtedly remove any savings they might have accumulated in this country, any surplus cash they might have, before they actually put a percentage of the stock on the Canadian market. John Meyer, a financial writer for a Montreal newspaper, has estimated that these savings might amount to as much as
Income Tax Act
$4 billion. This would, I feel, put the minister in a difficult position concerning his foreign exchange.
Another question that might be raised is, are Canadian funds actually available for the purchase of these equities if they are put on the Canadian market? Possibly some Canadian capital is available. However, in other cases those wishing to exercise their right to purchase some of these equities might have to borrow capital. They might go out of the country to borrow this capital. The interest payment on this borrowed capital might amount to more than the dividends if they had been left in the hands of the original holder.
I could go on, Mr. Chairman, pointing out these inequities. I should like, however, to give one small illustration in actual figures, which I believe to be true. As I understand it, if there is 76 per cent foreign ownership under the control of one person and 24 per cent Canadian, that particular company would have to pay the 20 per cent withholding tax. For the sake of argument, let us say a different company has 75 per cent held by one foreign person, 23 per cent held by another foreign person, and only 2 per cent Canadian. I understand, or my interpretation of the provision is, that this particular company would only pay the 10 per cent withholding tax. I suppose the company with the 76 per cent foreign control in one person and 24 per cent Canadian would be, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has put it in the past, considered to be the bad boys, whereas the company with 75 per cent foreign in one hand, 23 per cent foreign in another and only 2 per cent Canadian, would be considered the good boys. They would only pay the 10 per cent withholding tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? I will try to put it in the form of a question.
I would be glad to be corrected if I am wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then if I may correct the hon. member, 25 per cent of the stock would have to be listed on a Canadian stock exchange, the shares would have to be listed on the stock exchange, so Canadians would have an opportunity to buy them. The regulations of the exchange would require a substantial number of shareholders, or they would delist the stock.
Does the minister mean that 25 per cent would have to be listed on the Canadian stock exchange and that no foreigners could invest in it, only Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.

Income Tax Act

Then my original statement stands. I think a much more positive objection can be taken to this. My friends to the left may not agree, but I believe that consideration should be given to encouraging Canadians to invest in Canadian equities. We now have a situation where there is a deduction of 20 per cent on income tax on dividends received from Canadian corporations. Perhaps an increase in this amount could be considered as a positive approach. Another possible approach would be the broadening of the regulations under which insurance and trust companies are allowed to invest in equity stock. These provisions might create more Canadian interest in these equity securities and do it in a positive way rather than, as I claim, a discriminatory way which is going to discourage foreign capital investment which we feel is necessary.
This country is still young. The minister mentioned a moment ago the other sectors in which he indicated that perhaps he had not emphasized strongly enough the fact that he is trying to get foreign capital to come in here and invest in bonds rather than equities. I agree with this move. However, on the other hand he then penalizes them for investing in equities. Despite the fact that there may have been a day when other countries, for argument's sake, found that the borrowings on bonds, debenture debt with fixed interest rates was possible-despite this, I think that today if we want investment capital in Canada we have to give some encouragement.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that we are going completely in the wrong direction on this matter. I think this is unworkable. I do not see how the minister is going to regulate this. As I mentioned earlier, there was the one instance I pointed out of the 76 per cent foreign ownership on one hand and the 24 per cent Canadian, and that company still would have to pay the 20 per cent withholding tax. On the other hand the company with 75 per cent in one foreign interest, 23 per cent in other foreign hands and only 2 per cent Canadian would be considered the good boys and only pay the 10 per cent withholding tax. As one hon. member said, you do not even have to have 2 per cent Canadian, because all you have to have is 25 per cent of the stock listed on the stock exchange. You would not have to have any in Canadian hands, except for the qualifying directors.
As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has indicated in the past, this may well be a good field for lawyers. They will be receiving some great retainers. In fact at that time I would rather belong to that profession than the one to which the minister and I belong. There will be a gold mine

for the lawyers in the appointment of these dummy directors, and so on.
I reiterate, Mr. Chairman, that in my humble opinion one cannot regulate the flow of capital in this way. You cannot do it by legislation. I do not think it is logical. I feel that we are going to disrupt the whole business community, and we are going to frighten the business community. This has happened already. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the resolution brought forward by the Solicitor General I should like to say that it deals with a situation that has been before the house on many occasions in the last number of years. In that regard I refer not only to the last six or seven years but to many years before that.
I believe the main difficulty in the case of all the consumer credit bills now on the order paper is the question of jurisdiction. In each instance where the matter of consumer credit arises there has been a conflict as to the division of responsibility between the federal government, with its responsibility for interest, and the provincial governments with their responsibility for contracts of a personal nature. For that reason I hope if the resolution is passed and the committee is set up it will be composed of people who will be able to deal with the difficult constitutional problem.
After the constitutional problem is settled there is also the difficulty of passing legislation which will prevent people from being foolish at a time when they are badly in need of finances. All the bills on the order paper now, as well as previous bills, if they have been opposed when they have come up for discussion have been opposed on the ground that you cannot legislate common sense into people when they are making a contract. A person who is in a very difficult financial position is prepared to pay a large sum by way of interest in order to get the money which he badly needs at the time. It has always been another difficulty that if we legislate too stringently in connection with consumer credit it may dry up the legitimate source thereof and force people to other means of securing money when they require it.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, we also do not wish to hold up the resolution, so I would simply say we are prepared to support it. We hope the committee will make a very complete investigation of consumer credit. There are items of legislation in the provincial legislatures along the same line, and I feel we will have to consider the provincial legislation also to see that we do not overlap. But as I say, we are in support, in general terms, of this resolution.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. members of this group welcome the setting up of this committee because we believe it has before it an important task. The problem of credit is becoming increasingly important, both because of the fact that the amount of credit being used by the people of Canada is rising at an alarming rate, and also because of the fact that there is in this

Consumer Credit Committee business, as I suppose there is in every business, a small percentage of people who are so interested in making money that they really have no scruples or any friends. The newspapers of Canada from one end to the other have been filled with examples of people who have not only gone into debt to an extent they could not possibly afford, but in fact have been charged the most fantastic and exorbitant rates of interest. Recently the Financial Post carried a story about a recent immigrant to Canada who became the victim of a mortgage broker. This person borrowed $1,501 from the broker, and that is what he received; but he had to sign a note for $2,350, the extra $849 representing an arranging fee. After paying the prescribed $35 a month for three years he discovered that he still owed $1,580, which was more than he had borrowed in the first place. He was supposedly paying an interest rate of 7 per cent but he was in fact paying 30 per cent. There are dozens of cases on record along this line and there is no need that I list them.
This year the Ontario legislature appointed a select committee to inquire into the situation. They called before them mortgage brokers who testified that they had lent money on which they had charged interest rates of 80, 90 and 100 per cent. It is true the mortgage brokers claimed that they really did not know the interest rates. But that is not the important thing; the important thing is that people were forced to pay these rates.
I know this committee will have great difficulty, owing to the federal set-up of our country. Part of the responsibility for this question is federal and part is, of course, provincial. We had in the province of Manitoba until recently an act which provided for the orderly payment of debt. Under this act people who found they could not meet their obligations were able to go to court and were able to get the court to set the rate they could afford to pay their creditors, as well as the order in which they would pay. Within the last year or so the courts in Manitoba have ruled that that act was beyond the powers of the province and really came under the jurisdiction of the federal government. I think the committee should consult with provincial governments. They would also have the responsibility of calling in people who are in the credit business. I was going to say there may be people, but I think that is a little unfair: there are some legitimate people in this business, but there are some who are not. I do not think the whole business should be tarred with the same brush. I do not think the responsible and legitimate people should take, or indeed would want to take the responsibility for the misdeeds of the few. They should have the right 
to appear before this committee. For example, I saw recently a case where the head of a big acceptance company was arguing that the business had no objection to telling people what they would pay by way of return, but that it was impossible to state it in terms of simple interest. I disagree completely. However, the committee should hear all these people, and I hope when it reports back to the house the government will bring in legislation so that the kind of stories now prevalent from one end of Canada to the other, of people being gouged and mistreated, will disappear, and this whole practice be declared illegal and prohibited in the future.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to support the measure now before us proposing the setting up of a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons to inquire into and report on matters relative to consumer credit. We find today that many Canadians are placed in the paradoxical position of living in the midst of abundance, yet facing personal problems of poverty and in many cases destitution. We like to brag about our high standard of living, but on the other hand we must face the unpleasant fact that even in this country there are thousands living just above the borderline of destitution. I think this is an indictment of our society and the economic system which now operates.
We in the Social Credit party have always maintained that the amount of purchasing power in the hands of the people should fairly closely approximate the reasonable price of goods and services available. We believe that is essential if we are to maintain our economy at the proper level. At the present time this is not so. We find the income earned by our people is further drastically reduced by substantial rates of taxation at all levels of government, which further reduces the purchasing power of the people. I feel this entire problem needs real consideration, and we trust that the terms of reference of this committee will enable it to go into all these relevant fields.
I am sure that a survey of the homes in our nation would indicate a shortage of many of those appliances and other items which have become commonplace to many of us. On the other hand, as I have indicated, there is a superabundance of these items in our stores and factories. The result has been that in order to try and acquire these appliances many people have gone so far into debt that they almost find it impossible to extricate themselves. The temptation to buy on credit is, of course, very real. Walk down the streets of our cities and towns and see the neon signs everywhere proclaiming the fact that you

can come in and borrow money, on supposedly reasonable terms and under very pleasant circumstances. But we do find that this contributes to the position in which many of our people find themselves when they buy on credit to such an extent their income is not adequate to cover the payments they must make. So we find that credit buying runs to between $3 and $4 billion, which is a considerable amount of money.
We have a proliferation of companies who are engaged in credit operations, and we do not object to that fact. However, there is increasing concern over some aspects of the problem, and this has been pointed up by the number of bills currently on the order paper, the subject matter of which we have been assured will be referred to this proposed committee for consideration. Most of us have received letters and other communications calling attention to alleged unethical practices indulged in by some of these companies. As the previous speaker said, we do not want to tar all these companies with the same brush because many of them are carrying on in a very commendable manner; but there are some which are not. I have received a communication in which attention is drawn to one of these practices. I hope I can refer this to the committee for consideration during its hearings. A man bought a piece of equipment. He got behind in his payments once or twice and was charged, seemingly, an exorbitant rate of interest. He then carried on his payments satisfactorily. But when he had almost come to the last of his payments he was told he must have the complete amount ready in two days. This placed him in an enormous impossible situation.
Circumstances such as this do arise from time to time. I believe many of those who are now engaged in the financing business would, themselves, like to clear up such practices. Many of them are trying to carry on their operations in an ethical manner and are concerned about others who, by their sharp practices, bring discredit upon the lot. I welcome the proposal to set up this committee and for our part we shall give it our full support.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that this resolution on the appointment of a committee on consumers' credit is most welcome.
I can say without fear of being contradicted that Canada's economy depends on finance, on credits and on loans. The federal government is up to its neck in debt-if the simile may be forgiven-the provincial governments, or at least most of them, are carrying a much too heavy load of debts, and the
Consumer Credit Committee same thing applies to municipalities, school boards-one of my hon. colleagues says that the same situation prevails among members -and private citizens.
When a child is born, the happy father rushes to finance companies and borrows some money in order to buy a crib, diapers and feeding bottles. When the child is old enough to go to school, parents purchase various items on credit in the stores or by mail order catalogues, and get 36 or 48 months to pay on the instalment plan. When the time comes to go to college or to the university, finance companies are visited ones again.
And when the time comes to get married, money is borrowed either to buy a house, or to purchase furniture for the bedroom, the living room, or to buy a car or refrigerator.
Having reached 35 or 40 a man buys a house through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; he is allowed a period of 35 years to pay back his loan, so that he will be 75 or 80 by the time he becomes the owner of his house.
This thing has come to a point where morticians tell people: "Die now, pay later".
Mr. Speaker, such is the situation which prevails. Finance is with us from our birth to our death, and a person has to pay interest during his whole life. Our Canadian citizens do not know how to get out of it.
When a citizen, a small business or a small industry are in the hands of finance companies, they often have to pay extravagant interest rates and commissions.
I do not think it would be an exaggeration to say that in our region of Saguenay-Lake St. John, we have usurers who take advantage of the small people, the small worker and the small farmer, possibly to a greater extent than anywhere else in Canada. We have seen individuals who, in order to borrow $2,000, gave a commission of $1,000 and signed promissory notes for $3,000, so that in three or four years, they sometimes paid back up to $5,000.
It is when Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation refuses to lend money to farmers, that usurers take advantage of the situation. Finance companies will do the same when they lend money to an individual to buy furniture, a car, etc.
The time has come to put an end to all that, but when you take a look at the interest rate of the federal government, you must recognize that they too are excessive.
For instance, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is still lending money at 6] per cent, while chartered banks are prohibited by law from lending at more than 6 per cent. Therefore, I consider that the federal government sets a bad example by lending money at 6{ per cent.

Northwest Territories Act
The object of the act is to enable the little fellow to build a house, but the federal government is the first to take advantage of him by charging him 6j per cent interest, while forbidding the chartered banks to charge more than 6 per cent, which it considers a reasonable profit.
The same is true in regard to the industrial development bank which, in certain cases, charges up to 7 per cent interest. I think this is an excessive profit, and we should examine what the federal government is doing in this field.
We might also-and I just mention it incidentally-look into the credit situation of the chartered banks. It would be an opportunity for us to discover who is creating credit in Canada and why credit is such a scarce commodity.
The resolution will enable us to call and question witnesses, and we have the firm intention to question those who are creating and making credit in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, those are the remarks I wanted to make to point out that this committee is needed, and also to show up to what point we should go to establish credit sources while trying to delve into the problem.
I hope that all hon. members sitting on that committee will carefully consider the credit situation and see to it that a sensible solution of the problem is reached.
