He said: It is my intention in moving second reading of this bill to make a brief statement concerning the proposal which, taken together with the succeeding bill, is intended to bring a greater measure of self-government to the people of the Canadian north. I hope that if any of those who take part in this debate wander from the terms of this measure to the extent of discussing the bill which is to follow, you will pardon them, Mr. Speaker, because these two bills are part of the same plan.
Some members of the house probably think that we are creating history in Canada today when we propose to establish two new territories in this country. I hope there will be participation from all sides of the house
[Mr. GregoireJ
in the debate which is now to take place. We are dealing with the Northwest Territories, that remaining part of the Canadian frontier which is not within one province or another. I wish to remind hon. members, especially those who have not had the good fortune to visit this part of the country, what an almost unbelievable stretch of real estate we are discussing. This region embraces 1,300,000 square miles or about 34 per cent of all the land area of Canada. It is almost 1,800 miles from any corner, or any part, to the furthest opposite point of this vast territory. It is a region which we have found largely unmanageable even from a central position in Ottawa.
We have decided that the time has now arrived when an increasing amount of selfgovernment should be granted to the people who live there. We think the efficiency of government in every sphere will be improved by moving away from centralized government towards a position where there will be more government on the ground, as I have chosen to describe it. We think that in the territory as a whole the time has now arrived for us to extend a great new measure of authority so as to enable the inhabitants to conduct their own affairs. I say this in the light of the increasing investment in the north, the increasing population, the higher standards of education and the greater understanding among those who live there of the resources available and of what can be done with them.
It has been decided, therefore, to divide this immense territory into two parts. It is the thought of this government, as it was of the preceding government, that if self-government is to be extended to this region it must be brought to at least something like manageable size. In the proposals contained within these two bills consideration is first of all given, as one might expect, to the historic division of this great territory, that is its division by nature. For reasons which will be readily understood, we are paying particular attention to the facts of transportation. This is a country where transportation appears to me to be the limiting factor.
We have therefore, paid attention to the western side which we propose to call Mackenzie. Outlining the boundaries there, we have set them along the Mackenzie river and up to the border of the Arctic ocean. The division line is the 105th longitude of west meridian; proceeding from the 60th latitude northward until it reaches the Arctic circle, thence surrounding Victoria island and Banks island, to take in these two major islands. This is to be incorporated in the territory of Mackenzie.

Northwest Territories Act
I am satisfied that this particular area is quickly going to be able to take care of itself. It is preponderantly, with the exception of Victoria and Banks islands, below the tree line. I want to remind hon. members that when they go to the Arctic they will see the unbelievable significance of a tree line in this country. When you leave the tree line of Canada it is like having the water cut off. Indeed, there is a relationship between the tree line and water. The western part of Mackenzie, which we propose to set aside, is largely treed. It has a great many things in common with southern Canada. Within the next several years. I would think by October, 1965, it will have a railway to latitude 62.
I am delighted to know that as a result of amendments that were made to the Railway Act in 1952, the laid down cost of carlots in Hay River, as a result of the provision then passed that freight to all areas in Canada in carlots must not exceed one and one third times the transcontinental rate, will be the same rate as for a car landed at Calgary, Alberta. This is going to mean a tremendous result in my opinion, in that country. I think it will have the effect of supplying goods to the western north at a saving of $10 to $15 a ton. This, in turn, is going to have the effect of reducing the cost of living, reducing the cost of operation of companies in that area in search of minerals and of oil to the point that some properties which they judge to be uneconomic may well be brought into the economic sphere.
At Hay River, which was unfortunately badly devastated by a flood in May of this year, rebuilding has taken place. As I think I told the house last night, freight shipments on the Mackenzie, down to the mouth of the Mackenzie by water, are some 50 per cent higher in 1963 than they were in the shipping year of 1962. At latitude 62, or just below it, we have the huge investment in the Pine Point mine. It, too, will be served by the railway, which will have its terminus at Hay River, by a spur line taken off some few miles below Hay River and running east to Pine Point. An enormous expenditure is being made there by the parent company, something in the nature of $30 million, on a lovely townsite.
After you leave Great Slave lake and go down the Mackenzie, there are a great number of locations of increasing importance populated by people in increasing numbers who have confidence in their ability to stay there and make their way. I think that with the many treasures of the future in the Arctic, particularly in the western Arctic, tourism is going to be one of our great industries. I was glad to note that a private
company operating out of Hay River is setting in motion plans to have a tourist ship run on the Mackenzie river next year down to the Arctic. I would think it would be blessed with success from the start. It is exceedingly interesting country. One can, if he should get up, or should stay up, until 2 a.m. in the morning, still see the sun. There are situations there and people there of very great interest to Canadians from southern Canada.
In so far as the eastern Arctic is concerned, I must say at once that, due to the fact it is above the tree line, due to the fact that so far, in spite of investigations we have made, there do not seem to be comparable resources to those existing on the western side of the Arctic, the outlook for the future is more difficult. The fact is that, in spite of investigations made by our fisheries department and other departments, the amount of resources in the country seems relatively low in proportion to the people who are living there. Communication is exceedingly difficult. It is for this reason that in the bill respecting that part, in other words the residue of the territory left when we pass the Mackenzie bill, we have decided to retain the centre of government in Ottawa.
Let me remind hon. members that transport for officials, transport for those engaged in search of development of the country, is largely by airplane. It is costly and it is of such a nature in respect of the eastern Arctic that if one flies out of here, or from Toronto or Montreal to the north, there is no service either east or west to the various points up there. One has to come back to southern Canada and go from there to the next point in that country.
I do want to pay tribute to the indigenous people of the area. Canadians, by and large, did not know them 10 to 15 years ago. In the last 10 or 15 years, we have made a real effort to know them. Probably, in many cases, a selfish interest took us there because we were looking for resources other than people, but we found people there. I want to pay tribute to these people. I do not want to portray quite the terrible difficulties that were put before the house last night by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) who spoke of the unbelievable hardships with temperatures down below 50 or 55 degrees. I am as fully aware as he that the kind of average climate up there is not the climate that I saw in the months of August or September.
However, I believe that successive governments have done a good job of taking those things up there that we want to leave there and taking to these people an increasing measure of the amenities of life to protect them from the elements. I admit that there

Northwest Territories Act are quite a number of people, particularly on the eastern side of the Arctic, who today have no home to put over their heads; none whatever. There are probably-this is only my estimate based upon having made one visit-1,000 or 1,500 indigenous persons who have no shelter from the weather. In the future, Mr. Speaker, I am going to propose to members of this house that one of the prerequisites for talking to these Canadians will be that we talk to them out of the weather. I would propose to this house in the future that we should find some means of taking these unfortunate people in out of the weather, by the production of homes which we could put in there for a reasonable price.
I saw what I believe was called a 10 by 24. The hon. member for Northwest Territories may correct me if I am wrong. It is just that -a house 10 feet wide by 24 feet long. I saw, in a number of instances, not one, two or three families but probably four families living in that one house. I do not want members of parliament to decry that condition because that is better than having no house at all, a great deal better. I hope that in the future, in respect of these people, we can move into an era where we can say these Canadians have a home and shelter from the weather, in an area which does not have the most hospitable climate in Canada.
In addition to the extremely low temperatures, I am informed there are winds accompanying these temperatures. I was told that the winds range from 80 miles per hour to 100 miles per hour with temperatures many degrees below zero. There are Canadians who know far more about the north than I who say that, in the end, the eastern Arctic may come off best. When I was there this summer I saw them drilling for oil at latitude 75. I endeavoured last night to pay tribute to the companies who are putting risk capital into that area. One of these drilling companies expended $360,000 to bring their drilling equipment into the area. I think it behoves Canadians in every part of Canada to give some marks to these companies who are taking the risk in that territory, when they could invest money in southern Canada and have it secure.
I think that their contributions should be emulated by a great many more Canadians, and should be accepted by members of parliament in the spirit in which they are risking that capital. A great deal of money is in there searching for oil, and if they find the fields which geologists are confident are present, then there could be the situation that the real riches of the Arctic rest in the east instead of the west. If that should be the case I would be extremely happy because I am content in my own mind that the future of the western part of the Arctic is secure.
[Mr. Laing.l
I think our chief interest for some years to come is going to be in respect to the eastern Arctic.
I could go on to tell something about the populations. When these bills pass the house, and I hope they do quickly, as otherwise we will have no government in those territories, we will have in Mackenzie a territory so vast that there will be one person per 38 square miles, and in the territory of Nunassiaq we will have one Canadian per 200 square miles. The size of these areas is almost unbelievable, and their difficulties are great. The costs of doing or developing anything there are extremely high, and the problems of living in that climate are not easy.
I think these bills, supported by the council of the Northwest Territories by formal resolution at their council meeting in Inuvik in July this year, were developed not by this government but by our predecessors, out of resolutions passed by the council of the Northwest Territories, and I hope we move forward with them quickly as a very important new offer of self-government to the people in that area, to the extent that in the western area they will have a majority of elected members.
They will have a commissioner resident in the Mackenzie. They will have for the first time almost the same degree of self-government as the Yukon territory enjoys today, and I hope therefore, Mr. Speaker, we can move forward intelligently but expeditiously with these bills.

I did give that commitment in the name of the government and the government is not going to break its word, or even appear to be breaking its word, to any hon. member. But the government is not prepared to accept an amendment which, under the rules we operate under, would kill the bill. We cannot do that. If hon. members feel that they are committing themselves to any principle they do not want to commit themselves to, by voting for second reading of the bill before such reference is made to a committee, I am unable to say what day such a motion could be brought up or how soon it would be possible to set up that committee. All I am saying is that I will carry out the undertaking I gave to get some kind of motion on the order paper which we can take up whenever we can. In the meantime we will just leave the legislation on the order paper, because obviously we cannot do both things at once.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this very point, when the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) says that the request came from only one member I must draw his attention to the fact that as early as June 7 I had begun directing questions to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing). As reported on page 780 of Hansard I directed this question to the minister:
In view of the far reaching implications of this measure-
That is, the bill-
-to the people of the north, will the minister assure me, and through me the people of the north, that he and his colleagues will consider the establishment of a special house committee to examine this proposal, in consultation with the people of the north, who after all are the ones most affected by the measure?
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources replied at that time, in part:
I think that with regard to any possible change in the present policy of presenting bills to the house I will have to take the question as notice and make a further study. I may be doing that in a few days.
Subsequently the minister of northern affairs did suggest that this would be done.
On this topic generally, Mr. Speaker, I think I should point out to the house that, although parliament opened on May 16 of this year it was not until July 8 that the Secretary of State and house leader chose to introduce the resolution stage of this bill. I think hon. members should be aware that this was a mere 48 hours before the Northwest Territories council opened its sittings in Inuvik, Northwest Territories. At that time the house leader said to the house, in effect: "You must proceed with this immediately. Please don't debate it. We will give any kind of undertaking; we are short of time". I submit that there was no reason to be short of
Northwest Territories Act time, even at the resolution stage, because from May 16 the government knew the Northwest Territories council session opened July 10. It was left to within 48 hours of this event before the resolution was pushed through, with certain commitments. The commitments were that if any member of the house asked for a special committee the government would undertake to set one up. It would not have the effect of killing the
bin.
As recently as last night the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) gave a precedent in this regard. If reference is made to Hansard for May 14, 1946, the house leader of that day, the Hon. Ian Mackenzie, referred a bill on reinstatement in civil employment to a standing committee before reaching second reading stage, with the concurrence of the house and without having the effect of killing the bill.
I think it is most important with this kind of legislation that we realize that no one in this house is asking for the bill to be killed. We are merely asking, and have been ever since I got into this house on June 1, that some opportunity, some vehicle, be provided whereby residents of the Northwest Territories-who I must say are not all in agreement by any means that division of the north is a good thing-have an opportunity to be heard. There is a wide disparity of opinion on that question, from pretty eminent individuals such as a judge of the court of the Northwest Territories and a former Liberal member of this house who travels extensively through the north, and who has said categorically in press statements and in decisions to juries recently that division will be a bad thing. I merely point out some rather highly placed and eminent people peculiarly suited to understanding the implications of this issue have asked for a special committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, I am. I am pointing out to the Secretary of State, in connection with his assertion that any effort to cause extra inquiry to be made would be interpreted as an effort to kill the bill, that we categorically deny this is in the minds of any of the members on this side. Rather, we are acting in response to requests received from many people in the Canadian north.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:

Northwest Territories Act will have nothing before it except such a motion as I might draft. What objection is there to giving these bills second reading? That does not make them law. Let them go to the committee and be subject to as full an inquiry as is desired. The government is quite happy to have that done.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: The answer to that proposal is that many people in the north are not in agreement with the principle of the bill and they want to be heard. This does not mean the bills will not eventually be enacted. It merely means there is no point in going through a charade. What is the point of saying to them: "Come on down and let us know whether you think the north should be divided" when it has already been decided that this should be done, because approval has been given to the bill in principle.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
On the point of order, may I refer to the precedent referred to by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and tell the house that that involved a government bill, Bill 54 concerning the reinstatement of the civil employment act. A motion was moved that the bill be not read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to a select committee. We are, therefore, reinforced in our thinking that this is a sound practice, unless there has been a change in our standing orders which would preclude such a course from being considered.
I have not the latest edition of Beauchesne, but I have the third edition, and at page 498 reference is made to a similar incident. An act to amend the Railway Act was introduced by the government and in the course of the debate an amendment was proposed that the subject matter be referred to a committee. The Speaker, I think it was Mr. Speaker Black, ruled that this was a valid amendment. An appeal was made from his decision, but the decision was sustained. This is to be found on page 501. If the only fear of the Secretary of State is that a motion of this kind will kill the bill, I think his misgivings might be allayed by these precedents.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I ask the honourable and learned gentleman a question? He knows I have the greatest respect for his knowledge of the rules, a knowledge which I think is much greater than, my own. But I was not arguing that a motion to refer the subject matter of the bill to a committee would be out of order. I recognize, as I imagine does everybody else, that it would be in order. But I say it would, none the less, kill the bill.
Let the hon. member ask this question: What would the committee do? The committee would no longer have the bills before it. There would be nothing to come back to this

house but the report of the committee- no bill upon which this house could proceed. In some fashion, another bill would have to be introduced and we would have to start all over again with another resolution. The other bill might be identical in language to the one before us now, but it would have to be introduced with a resolution preceding it, it would have to be given first reading and second reading and then go to committee again. That is a process which this government believes to be totally redundant and this is why I ask the hon. member for the Northwest Territories what objection he has to our sending this bill to the committee, together with the other bill. The house can still defeat them on third reading if it wishes to do so. The committee could keep them in committee indefinitely, if that is its wish. Every argument could be used in committee precisely as it could be used if the subject matter of the bills were sent to it. But the bills themselves would be intact, so that after the committee had done its work they could come back to the house as bills, if the committee wanted them to go back, and be considered by this house.
If any hon. member wants to hold me to the undertaking I gave in the name of the government on July 8, that we would suspend this legislation but that I would draft a motion and put it on the order paper, a motion having to do in particular with the islands referred to by the hon. member for Lapointe, and with the question whether the territory should be divided at all, we should be ready to do that. However, I think it should be clearly understood what the consequences would be. It is not reasonable to hope that this legislation could possibly get through during this session of parliament. That process would inevitably involve delays. It would involve putting on the order paper a motion giving 48 hours' notice and it would mean finding parliamentary time in which to discuss the matter. Yet we could get the whole thing through the committee in ten minutes, right now, if we had a mind to, and it would not commit us to anything more. I appeal to the hon. member who, I feel, is conscientiously trying to represent his constituents to let the bills be given second reading. Let them go to the committee and then let us take all the time necessary.

This is an omnibus bill containing a number of amendments. There are some with which I am in perfect agreement. With others, I am not. Consequently, I find it difficult to say I am in agreement with this bill in principle. This is why I put forward the suggestion I have just advanced.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-29, to provide for the development of certain provinces by the distribution of industry and for the reduction of unemployment therein.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it has been some time since I first introduced this bill, and in the interim steps have been taken by both governments, which have been of some benefit in providing tax incentives to various areas which have had high unemployment for a long period of time. However in my opinion the decent step of designating certain specific areas that will provide certain benefits for industries that locate within them, is too little and too late, from a maritime point of view.
We must take very comprehensive, realistic and bold steps that will give a guarantee of revitalizing the economy of the Atlantic provinces by ensuring that industries will look upon the area with interest because of the incentives provided. I do not feel that selecting certain areas in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is going to do the job. I do not think it is very realistic for a government to tell the people of Prince Edward Island that they have no area within which incentives should be provided for the location of new industries, and that they should go it alone and try to compete against other areas in the Atlantic region because these other areas are faced with more severe problems than they are.
Only recently the Atlantic provinces economic council placed this matter before the royal commission on taxation, and stated that if areas were to be designated, then the whole Atlantic provinces should be designated as an area where special and very broad tax incentives should be provided. Certainly nothing government has said or done to date is as comprehensive as the action that would be forthcoming if the bill I have introduced were adopted.
I believe the statement made by the present Minister of Fisheries, (Mr. Robichaud) when

this subject was last debated in the house, should be looked at closely. I look forward to hearing from him in this debate later on. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, (Mr. Martin) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) also took part in that debate, and were most anxious to see the government of that day adopt it. I hope the Minister of Fisheries will fortify the remarks he made on that occasion and, as a result of the persuasion he must have with his colleagues, see to it that the bill is adopted today instead of being talked out.
There is much to be done in the Atlantic provinces, and there is much that can be done if the purpose that is embodied in this bill is adopted. I look forward to its being adopted by the government and to seeing great new development take place in the Atlantic provinces because of the incentives inherent in the bill.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to place on the record a portion of an editorial which appeared in the Fredericton Daily Gleaner of November 5, which says in effect what we need in the Atlantic provinces in the way of special tax incentives:
The federal government's tax concession policy, if it can be called that, is to pick a few scattered communities, declare them as high unemployment areas, and then give "qualifying" industries establishing in them a three-year corporate tax exemption. That is a most inadequate way of dealing with the economic ills of the Atlantic provinces. Such a policy stands about as much chance of checking rising unemployment as a popgun has of stopping a charging rhino.

This is no example of steps that are going to revitalize the economy of our Atlantic provinces. With reference to the point of order which has been raised I have serious doubts as to the legality of the bill. It is true that when the industrial development bank was constituted it was not preceded by a resolution. However the Bank of Canada, which subscribes to the shares of the industrial development bank, was itself incorporated in 1934 by an act which was preceded by a long resolution. Furthermore, the last time the Industrial Development Bank Act was amended, as set out in chapter 50 of the statutes of 1960-61, the amending bill was preceded by a long resolution which began with the words: That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act to enlarge the classes of loans that may be made under the act so as to include therein all business enterprises without limitation of the kind of business carried on-
In Bill C-29 now before the house there is provision to allow the bank to make grants or loans toward providing basic services and toward the establishment or assistance of an industrial enterprise. Furthermore, there is provision that the bank may make grants or loans in an area of persistent high-level unemployment and to relax their restrictions at the bank's discretion as to the type of enterprise and conditions of assistance. If it were thought necessary in 1961 that the measure to amend the act so as to enlarge the classes of loans which could be made should be preceded by a resolution, I am not sure that a similar measure could now be introduced by a private member in a different manner. It is true that in 1961 there was also an increase in capital from $25 million to $50 million; also an authorization to increase the borrowing authority of the bank, and other provisions. To say the least, this is a borderline case, but since the discussion has already started I will authorize a discussion of the bill. But I must indicate the

possible difficulties that a bill of this kind will present and that the same bill will not be taken as a firm precedent for similar legislation. I would consider it proper for the discussion, since it has started, to continue.

Ottawa, February 1, 1963.
Dear Mr. Mayor:
I know my colleague, the Honourable Walter Dinsdale, has been in touch with you in regard to the same matters as you raised in your letter to me of January 10th. I am informed that the Northwest Territories council favours Fort Smith for the capital of the proposed new territory of Mackenzie when it is organized.

I am.
Yours sincerely, John G. Diefenbaker
