speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing the estimates of the Department of Labour I should like to make as brief as possible a statement on the work of the department. Members of the committee will realize that in the course of this session labour matters have received quite exhaustive treatment, and that the opportunities which have been provided on two supply motions, and in the debate on the trusteeship legislation, will not make it necessary for me to enter into the detail that might be necessary in the absence of these other opportunities.
On Tuesday of this week the house as a whole had an opportunity to deal with quite

a number of matters relating to the Department of Labour. It will be my endeavour not to duplicate what was said on that occasion. I will confine my remarks to putting to the committee some views on the activities of the department as a whole. Last Tuesday I told hon. gentlemen that when introducing my estimates I would make a general statement with respect to the Minister of Labour's responsibilities in connection with employment and unemployment.
I think that in the house, and elsewhere throughout the country, the Minister of Labour tends to be held responsible, sometimes one would think exclusively, for the problems of employment and unemployment, and I thought I might indicate my conception of the role of the minister in this important field. First of all, I would suggest that the Minister of Labour has the responsibility for reporting to the House of Commons on the level, character and source of unemployment.
He also has a primary responsibility, working with other groups, for the development, adaptation and efficient utilization of manpower resources, and effective measures of this kind can contribute to the promotion of employment and to the prevention or reduction of unemployment. In addition the minister and his department can help contribute to this reduction or prevention by encouraging short run measures to create employment opportunities. These are clearly responsibilities which fall mainly on the Department of Labour.
To move to a broader sphere, it must be understood that so far as unemployment results from a failure of demand to employ fully all available and qualified labour supplies-and this is the case to some extent today-the Minister of Labour's responsibility for the level of unemployment, so far as the federal government is concerned, is shared with his colleagues. Primarily, responsibility for government action to stimulate demand sufficiently and to promote long term economic growths, rests with the government as a whole.
Several major government measures to help stimulate the economic growth of the country have already been discussed in the House of Commons. Opportunities arising from the minister's primary responsibilities in relation to unemployment and economic growth involve the training and development of the nation's youth to meet the requirements of the economy, the upgrading and training of the labour force to meet industrial and economic change, and the development of measures to create more employment opportunities at specific periods such as the winter, when seasonal unemployment is high.
28902-5-292
Supply-Labour
The young people now in our educational and training systems will need to be equipped for the rapid changing conditions characteristic of the Canadian economy in an age of technological and industrial change. This will involve continuing assistance by the federal government to support the provinces in developing technical training programs for youth and adults. This is a necessary form of investment as an integral part of the process of economic growth and employment creation. A well trained and adaptable labour force not only is a necessary element of growth but also plays a role in stimulating growth itself.
Rapid economic and technological changes today require great ability on the part of employed workers to adapt and adjust in order not to be replaced as their skill and educational levels become inadequate. If the labour force is not upgraded and adjusted to changing employment requirements, a greater volume of structural unemployment will accumulate. Therefore active programs in cooperation with the provinces are essential ways to upgrade the employed, and the training of the employed labour force to facilitate its adaptation to technological change. Seasonal unemployment will continue to push up total unemployment in Canada, particularly in the winter months, and there is scope for further governmental action in this field. Similarly cyclical unemployment will continue to be a problem and will require short term direct action to create employment in slack periods. The formulation and execution of manpower and development programs of these kinds clearly require a close working arrangement with other government departments and agencies on all levels and with non-governmental groups. Similarly, the Department of Labour must maintain a close consultative relationship with these public and private agencies and develop those aspects of government economic and social policy which have an important bearing on employment and manpower resources.
Finally, the Minister of Labour has important statutory responsibilities for carrying out research and current analyses of manpower development, employment and unemployment in the Canadian economy. These include undertaking research and presenting appropriate information and observations designed to assist in the formulation of government policy in this area. It also involves informing the public in an objective manner of current and future labour market and employment developments.
I should now like to turn to a number of specific activities for the current fiscal year. The committee will be asked to provide $220,831,000 in the main estimates, $47,967,000

Supply-Labour
in supplementary estimates A and $60,650,000 in supplementary estimates D. Of this total the Department of Labour itself requires $225,998,000 and the unemployment insurance commission $103,449,000. The combined figure for the Department of Labour and the commission represents a decrease of approximately $30 million over the 1962-63 main and supplementary estimates. In referring to the 1962-63 estimates I should point out that the final supplementary estimates for 1962-63, which totalled $62 million, are not shown on page 176 of the blue book which hon. members have before them. These supplementary estimates were released after the main estimates were printed.
I should also like to bring to the attention of members of the committee a reduction which I think is possible under item 30 of the main estimates. This item can be reduced by $5,000. Instead of requesting $525,700 as appears in the printed estimates, a careful review of our cash requirements indicates we shall require $520,700. This reduction of $5,000 is to be made in the primary vote, payments to provinces pursuant to federal-provincial farm labour agreements, which appears on page 183 of the details of services.
A word about administration. The first vote covers the costs relating to the general administration of the Department of Labour, international affairs and the women's bureau. Item 5 in the estimates makes financial provision for the activities of the economics and research branch. Research in the Department of Labour plays a key role in illuminating the complex manpower and industrial relations problems which we face and in providing a sound, factual basis in the development of programs and policies. The branch is the central federal agency for analysis and research in the labour field. It conducts major surveys and studies of wages and working conditions, union organization, collective bargaining, professional manpower and employment and unemployment. The results of these studies are made available not only to the government but to labour and management groups, to international agencies and to the public generally through the Labour Gazette and the many special reports and publications issued by the branch.
In its activities the economics and research branch is to an increasing extent developing studies of departmental programs such as municipal winter works and training of the unemployed in order to assist in evaluating their effectiveness in helping to improve job creating potential.
I would ordinarily have a great deal to say about the industrial relations activities of the department, especially in an effort to
[Mr. MacEachen.l
provide a current review of major industrial relations problems, but in view of the rather full discussions we have had in the house, particularly in connection with the longshoremen's strike and the developments on the great lakes, it may be that it would be possible for me to allow members of the committee to ask specific questions with respect to the activities of the industrial relations branch.
It might be of interest to members of the committee to learn that an encouraging report has come out of Chicago today with respect to the possibility of restricting or eliminating the picketing of Canadian ships at that port and elsewhere. I am informed that the labour relations board of the United States has held discussions with the labour bodies in that country, especially the S.I.U., and that there is a strong prospect that some success will be had in overcoming the picketing in the port of Chicago and elsewhere. I do not have all the details nor a complete picture of the situation, but I thought I should indicate to the committee that there is at least an encouraging indication this afternoon with respect to this continuing problem which has exercised the attention of members of the House of Commons for some months now.
If I may refer to civilian rehabilitation, because of the relative newness of this program, item 25 of the estimates provides for the financial needs of the civilian rehabilitation branch which administers the provisions of the Vocational Rehabilitation of Disabled Persons Act. This act came into effect on April 1, 1962. New federal-provincial agreements under the act have been signed with nine provinces. Under this legislation the branch co-ordinates the activities of federal government departments and assists provincial governments as required in the establishment, development and operation of the national rehabilitation program for disabled persons. The branch collects and disseminates information regarding rehabilitation methods and services and maintains liaison with the provincial authorities, voluntary agencies and professional associations regarding rehabilitation services for the disabled.
Through the program an increasing number of disabled Canadians are being enabled to lead more useful and satisfying lives independent of public assistance or financial help from relatives. In the past few years the program has restored almost 10,000 disabled Canadians to usefulness. This group and their 6,300 dependents were costing annually more than $6J million for support. Collectively they now earn almost $18 million annually. In the period covered, without the benefit of vocational rehabilitation services they would have cost almost $24J million. Instead they have

earned more than $63 million in that period.
Earlier in the week I covered a large number of the special programs of the Department of Labour, including the municipal incentive winter works program and other new programs, and unless hon. members wish to ask questions I have no intention of holding up the committee by a discussion of items that have already been covered recently, especially this week.
Items 35 and 40 of the main estimates can be dealt with together because they provide for the technical and vocational training programs. These are well known programs in which hon. members have taken a very keen interest. Hon. members will have noticed that there is before us on the order paper a resolution providing for certain changes in the program with respect to capital costs and the contributions made by the federal government for the training of the employed and the training of the unemployed, and because the house as a whole will have an opportunity to go into these particular programs in detail when the resolution and bill come before it. I do not intend to go into detail in my statement. I would be pleased however to answer whatever urgent questions hon. members should like to ask this evening. I do not pass over discussing this matter in detail because of any lack of regard for its importance, but simply because hon. members will have an opportunity later to deal in detail with all these matters as they debate the resolution and the bill.
There is nothing further I wish to add in making my opening statement to members of the committee, because we dealt with so many programs of the Department of Labour earlier in the week that it might be better for the minister, in the interests of time and economy, to set a good example and not take any longer this evening in opening the debate.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks in respect of the estimates of the labour department will be somewhat similar to those made by the Minister of Labour, because it is our intention to pass these estimates without any undue delay, although with careful examination. I only hope there are no obstructions from the government side in the expedition of these estimates, because I noticed as recently as last night that the minister of northern affairs, who had his estimates before the house, managed to talk them out and did not get them passed.
The Minister of Labour said that unemployment was dealt with exhaustively on Monday and Tuesday on the motion to go into supply. It is not our intention to deal tonight with this subject, because it was discussed on Monday and Tuesday, but I do not agree 28002-5-292i
Supply-Labour
with him that it has been gone into exhaustively. There will be ample opportunity, either in this session or the following one, for unemployment to be gone into exhaustively by the opposition.
At this time I should like to say that in my opinion, and in the opinion of other hon. members of the official opposition, the passing of supply is probably the most important business of the house. It is necessary that money be voted for the running of the country, and at times we find that other business comes before the consideration of supply. I think this is a mistake and I am sure the government will try to correct the error.
I do not intend to question the items listed in the estimates because I had some small part in their compilation, but I do want to make some remarks about certain matters which I noticed when I had this portfolio. The labour department has been considered in the past a poor cousin of all other governmental departments, but in the last five years or so I think its prestige has risen tremendously, until it now ranks as one of the most important departments of government administration. When I became minister of labour we had a yearly budget of something like $26 million, but it has risen to ten times that amount, simply because the labour department took on the responsibility of capital projects to help alleviate the unemployment situation, particularly during the winter months.
The minister made some remarks to the effect that he should not be responsible for the unemployment situation. I do not want to go into past history, but it is strange how one's attitude can change when responsibility rests on one's shoulders. I am glad to hear that this attitude has now been adopted, because when I was minister for some five and a half years it seemed to me as though I was a target for the unemployment situation by hon. members now on the government side, when they were in opposition.
The Minister of Labour mentioned that short term measures can be taken by the labour department to deal with unemployment during the winter months. This is entirely my idea, because during my term of office the labour department took many short term measures to deal with the situation. The minister also mentioned that during the winter months the seasonal aspect of unemployment will rise again, and has a tendency to raise the percentage of the unemployed over the whole year. While I agree with him entirely, this is exactly the sort of thing I tried to point out to the opposition when I was minister, but they paid no heed and treated the matter as though it were a year-round situation. However, there is a change

Supply-Labour
of attitude when you have responsibility, as I can readily understand, and I hope when the hon. member and his colleagues are back on this side of the house they will remember that burden of responsibility.
As I mentioned before, in the last five years the labour department has become one of the most important departments in government administration. I say this not because the departmental heads are in the gallery but because it was a great privilege to work with such a fine group of departmental officials. They were most helpful and one certainly does not need to prod them into action.
I think they accept responsibility willingly and with enthusiasm. During my five years of office we took on some large programs, such as the technical and vocational school building program, municipal winter works and the stepping up of a "Do it now" program which certainly has considerable merit. The training of the unemployed is, I think, one of the most important areas to which we should put our minds in order to help bring employment to the country. When I was told that 70 per cent of our labour force attained only grade eight education or lower it was an appalling shock to me. It was evident then that we should provide facilities and proper training for the labour force, simply because jobs available nowadays require 70 per cent skilled labour and 30 per cent unskilled. This 30 per cent is growing smaller each year, and consequently we must measure up to the demands of labour and endeavour to provide the necessary trades and skills demanded today.
Automation is another area, and it is interesting to recall that a study was made of this question, not only in Canada but in the United States. We should be very conscious of the fact that in Canada automation may be replacing workers at the rate of 2,500 people per week. Consequently we should take some steps to remedy that situation. It is regrettable that the government has not seen fit to put forward the bill which we had on the order paper dealing with manpower adjustment and automation. The government is going to deal with this matter by agreement. I feel that if they are to do this they should call a national conference of labour and management. I think you have to "sell" a program to people who are going to participate in it. You have to generate enthusiasm for it among those who will benefit as a result. It is not enough just to sign an agreement with the provinces and have so much money available for this program from the federal treasury. I think you have to "sell" the program in one way or another. I regret that this bill has not been put forward again, because I think it
IMr. Starr.]
would have sold this idea to those who would benefit from it. Even though the government has decided that the problem should be dealt with through agreement, I suggest to the minister that he consider holding a conference of employers and employees in order to discuss the merits of such a proposal.
With regard to industrial relations, this section of the department has always been very interesting to me. It is exciting, in that you deal with disputes in the country. I want to remind the committee that for the past six years now we have had no disruption of our national transportation system, and in this regard I think a great deal of credit must go to the head of the industrial relations department and his officers throughout Canada for their efforts to bring about this situation, or to at least hold the situation without suffering a further disruption. I might mention that during my term of office we had two very difficult situations to settle. One of these was concerning diesel locomotive firemen on freight and yard operations.
It had to be done in two stages, first on the Canadian Pacific and second, on the Canadian National systems. This was done successfully and without disrupting our transportation system. If we look across the border we find the same situation has been dragging out there for well over a year, possibly for two years, and that no settlement is in sight. A great deal of credit should be given for this. In the annual report of the department, mention is made of the settlement of a dispute involving 110,000 non-operating employees of the railway. For the first time in history the recommendations of the conciliation board were unanimously adopted. This was a historic occasion because, ordinarily, it is not done. I hope this is an indication of things to come and that from now on there will be an understanding that the report of the conciliation board shall be adhered to by both sides without the government being asked to deal with these questions. I think this is a matter for the parties concerned, and it is up to them to devise a system by which they can reach agreement.
I said earlier that training of the unemployed was most important. We took steps in 1960 to give an impetus to training of this type. If I remember correctly, the number of those trained in 1960 was 4,000. At the end of 1962, because of the impetus we had given to this program, the number had risen to 138,000. That is still not enough but it is certainly an improvement on the figure for 1960-almost ten times as many. This program should be continued so as to provide proper training for those who need to learn new skills.

The municipal incentive program, a new program which is only in its sixth winter, is a worth-while program. I shall not deal with it at any length except to read from the annual report, which says:
The municipal winter works incentive program during the 1962-63 winter provided an estimated 6,170.000 man-days of on-site work for an estimated 145,200 men. The previous winter's program had provided 5,870,000 man-days work for 147,700 men.
So this is a good program even though it was originally criticized. I went into some detail in respect to it during the debate on Monday and Tuesday. These are all the remarks I wish to make with respect to the estimates at this time. As I said earlier, I hope the government co-operates in getting these estimates passed as quickly as possible, the usual care being given to the expenditures involved.

The minister made such a good beginning in helping to settle the longshoremen's dispute, and then in getting legislation passed with respect to the seaway union, that I was really disappointed by his introduction to the estimates of his department tonight. Gone are all the speeches in which we were told what the government was going to do to solve the unemployment problem. Gone were the promises we heard for so many years about what the Liberal party and Liberal minister would do for labour. We gather tonight, from what the minister had to say, that all he has to do is to administer a department which is doing everything necessary to meet the situation.
I intend to refer to certain measures which are badly needed and to which no reference was made tonight. We need some major changes in our labour legislation. We need some major new acts, some of which members of the Liberal party, when they sat on this side of the house last year, indicated they were ready to support. We hoped the government would bring in this legislation. I certainly hope the minister would give some indication about his intentions tonight. For example, this country needs a new fair wages act providing for union wages and conditions on all government contracts, covering both prime contractors and subcontractors. We need a maximum work week act providing for a 40-hour week. I am told that in 1919 spokesmen for the Liberal party promised to bring in a maximum work week act. Well, a long time has gone by since then but still no action has been taken. We need a national minimum wage act providing for a minimum wage of $1.25 per hour. Last year members of this group introduced a bill on these lines. It received support from the Liberal party of that time, but there is little indication of any action being taken on it by the government
Supply-Labour
in the near future. We need an amendment to the holidays with pay act. This proposal, again, received support from hon. members opposite last session. We should like to see the government proceed to bring in such amendments. We need amendments to the provisions of the Criminal Code which deal with the right to picket. We need amendments to those parts of the code which deal with trespass.
We also need real amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Workers in Canada, under the protection of this act and under the protection of the various labour relations acts in the provinces, are guaranteed the right to join trade unions. Employers are forbidden to dismiss workers who have joined unions or to penalize employees for belonging to unions. In fact, these are nothing but theoretical rights. Every year during the last ten years hundreds of workers across Canada have been fired by their employers because they were foolish enough to believe that the laws of Canada mean what they say, and that they could join unions without the risk of losing their jobs. In fact, employers have ignored the provisions of the act in this respect. Indeed, it seems that we have one law for the rich and another for the poor; one law for the strong and another for the weak. If a person commits an offence against the law, if he robs a bank, or steals a car, or sells liquor illegally the police will apprehend him and prosecute him. But if an employer breaks the law, what happens? The worker or his union is required to make a complaint to the labour relations board. After hearing the details of the case, the board may behave in a very magnanimous way; it can give the worker or his union the right to prosecute.
I do not need to tell the committee or the minister how useless this procedure is. It takes time, it takes money, and then the case must be presented before a judge who often knows little or nothing about labour legislation. Even when an employer is found guilty, the penalty is usually of such a minor character that all it amounts to is a licence to go on breaking the law.
There was a case in Winnipeg a couple of years ago which illustrates this point. A brewery workers union organized a PepsiCola plant in the city. The company did what so many other companies have done-they fired a number of the key people working in the plant who were active in the union. The union got the provincial attorney general to take action against the company under the relevant provision of the Criminal Code. The case was brought before a magistrate and the company was found guilty. What did the

Supply-Labour
magistrate do? He assessed against the company a fine of $100. This, of course, was of no use to the union. It did nothing to protect the workers. In fact, the union was wiped out.
It seems to me that what we need is a thorough revision of our federal law and of the provincial labour acts, so as to give our labour relations board the authority which the national labour relations board has in the United States-the right to issue an order to a company to cease from discriminating against workers, and the right to issue an order for the reinstatement of workers who have been dismissed. The board should have the right to say to a company: You should not have fired this employee and you must pay his back wages during the time he has been unemployed. Without this kind of amendment to the labour laws of Canada, it seems to me that these laws are really only a snare and a delusion. In fact, they only create difficulties for the workers who believe that we mean business when these laws are passed. Until we pass this kind of legislation, both federal and provincial, the workers are not going to get the rights which, in fact, they have been promised.
It seems to me that not only should the federal government introduce this kind of amendment, but it should take the lead in calling a meeting of the various provincial labour departments to seek the passage of this kind of legislation in other provinces.
Now, I want to deal with another provision which has been extremely harmful to the workers and trade unions of this country. I refer to the provision of the Criminal Code which deals with trespass. As a result of this section of the code, trade unions have been denied access to workers on great projects all across this country. The workers in the lumber camps of Quebec and Ontario, the workers at Benson mines at Blind River, the workers at Seven Islands, the workers on the great International Nickel project at Thompson, as well as workers in other areas where companies have obtained concessions to develop great resources, have been denied their rights. In some of these areas the housing is provided by the company and is located on company property. The company uses this excuse, that the workers are living on their property. They say that this is private property and union organizers are denied the right of access to the workers on these projects.
They were building a power plant at Kelsey in the province of Manitoba, and employing in the neighbourhood of 2,000 workers for two years. It was completely impossible for trade unions to get in to talk to these workers during that time. The place was completely isolated and the only way one could get in

was by railroad on a spur line off the Hudson Bay railroad. You could not get in there without a pass from the company. Naturally, the company would not permit any union organizer to go in there. I have sworn affidavits to prove that the workers were compelled to work as much as 100 hours a week for six months at a time. If they did not do so, they were told they would be dismissed. The fact is the employees worked these hours without any overtime paid, without any of the benefits they would have received had a trade union been there. The union was unable to get in before the project was completed.
Similarly at Thompson where the International Nickel Company gained control of a hundred square miles through an agreement with the Manitoba government, for a period of almost two years the trade unions were completely prohibited from entering that area. Not only trade unions but members of parliament, members of the legislature, were prohibited. At that time I was a member of the legislature. I want to tell the members of this committee that it took me about a month, going from minister to minister, from deputy minister to deputy minister, before I finally went into the area without getting permission. The local government administrator, supposedly working for the government of Manitoba, was in fact an employee of the International Nickel Company. He simply refused to let me or any union organizer enter. I got in by telling him I was going in and if he wanted to get the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to take action, he could do so, but I would refuse to pay any fine which the court might assess and I was prepared to go to jail. Of course, at that point they acceded to my request, because it would not have looked very good for International Nickel.
This is the kind of thing which companies are doing consistently. As we move to develop our resources in the north, we are going to see more and more of this type of thing. One of these days the unions are going to say that they are not concerned with the law because the law is being misused. They are going to exercise the rights supposedly granted to them under our labour laws. They are going to enter one of these areas, and there is going to be trouble; there is going to be violence. Perhaps after we have that kind of violence the government of Canada will wake up and pass the kind of amendments to the Criminal Code which are required to deal with trespass. I would think we would be wise enough to pass this kind of amendment before we have that kind of trouble.
There is one other provision with which I want to deal, and that is the use of injunctions under the labour relations acts, both federal and provincial. Workers have a right to strike. I know people become disturbed

when we have strikes, and that is understandable. Many people in Canada do not realize that 99.5 per cent of the labour agreements are renewed without strikes. We only hear about the times when there are difficulties, when there are strikes. In Canada, because of the labour laws we have, it is more difficult and takes longer to get into a position where you can legally strike than in almost any other democratic country. I am not going to discuss at this time whether this is good or bad. This is part of the heritage bequeathed to this country by that great labour statesman, Mr. Mackenzie King. There is this whole business of the need to have bargaining in good faith between employer and employee, the need to call in a conciliation officer; and if you do not reach an agreement the need under the law to establish a conciliation board, before a trade union can go on strike. Anyone who has worked in this field knows how long it can take before a conciliation board can reach any kind of agreement or get to the point where they make their report.
If a union does all these things, if it does get into a position where it can strike, and even if it is a legal strike, Mr. Chairman, injunctions may be taken out. Even though the Criminal Code sets out clearly what is legal in the form of picketing, we have an increasing number of employees going to the courts to seek an injunction before there is any difficulty, before there has been any illegal action. A few days later they go to the court and get these temporary injunctions made permanent. The courts, in fact, are rewriting the law by their decisions, and picketing is virtually becoming illegal. Recently there was a strike in the city of Ottawa which happened to concern a building project of this federal government. The employees of one of the subcontractors went on strike, legally and properly, as they were entitled to do. They established a picket line around the job, since that was the only way they could inform people they were on strike. The company went to the court and got an injunction. The judge granted the injunction on the grounds that in picketing this place they were also picketing the prime contractor whose workers were not on strike. The argument of the lawyer for the union to the effect that if they did not picket this site where they were working, they could not picket at all, was simply ignored by the judge.
I suggest that if this government means business they had better get busy and rewrite the provisions of the Criminal Code so that union workers who find it necessary to go on strike will have their rights protected. I think it would be a good idea if the Minister of Labour were to convey to the various
Supply-Labour
provincial ministers the idea of making a survey to see how many injunctions against picketing there actually have been in the various provinces in the past number of years.
These are some of the things which I hoped the minister would talk about in the field of labour relations legislation. I should like to spend a few minutes talking about the Department of Labour. When I say things which I shall say, I am certainly not being critical of the people who are working or have been working for the department. I think they do an excellent job when one considers the staff they have and the scope which they are given. It seems to me that if we are going to function properly in the complex urban society in which we are living, we have to do a better job of equipping the people of Canada to get and hold jobs which will be available in this country. In order to do this, it seems to me a number of things are necessary.
First of all, you have to reorganize our educational system for this century, to make it effective, rather than making it the kind of educational system which fitted us for the last century. It is not my intention to go into detail tonight. We are all happy with the beginning which has been made in the field of vocational training. However, can the minister tell us what has happened to the people who have taken training in these new vocational training schools? Have they been able to find jobs? Have we been training them in the right skills? I am certain the minister cannot tell us, because we have not yet set up that kind of research organization which we ought to have in the Department of Labour. We ought to have a much greater technical training program at all levels, beginning with the grade six level and going right up to the university level.
When we read what is happening in the United States, and when we read the summary-because that is all we have had a chance to see-of the Robbins commission report in Great Britain, I am sure the minister will agree that what we have undertaken up to now is really a very meagre program. I am not critical when I say this. We have at least made a beginning, but I would hope that in the not too distant future the government, in co-operation with the provinces, will undertake a basic examination of what is needed and stop using the excuse that it is the provinces' responsibility. Let us co-operate in building a technical training program which would meet our needs, and to do these things we require a different kind of department of labour than the kind we have had up until now.
I believe it was the former minister of labour who said the labour department used

Supply-Labour
to be the poor department of government. I think it is still the poor department, but it should be the most important department of government. The department has a role to play which it has never accomplished because we have never given it the tools to do the job.
The department has to stop being mainly a quiet referee in the field of industrial disputes. It should be made the major department of the government, and should be given the main responsibility to secure adequate employment and decent wages for every Canadian.
I was disappointed with the speech the minister made the other day, when he was proud of the fact that we have some 10,000 less unemployed than we had this time last year. Of course that is better than having 10,000 more unemployed; but in the year 1963 to have a quarter million people unemployed is a disgrace to the country, to the government and to parliament. It is something we ought not permit to continue.
If we are to achieve the aim of full employment, then the labour department should be given the job of taking over and reorganizing the national employment service. It should make that service an aggressive, forward looking instrument of public service. So long as the employment service remains at the tail end of the unemployment insurance commission it cannot do a good job. If anyone thinks it is doing a good job, then let him take a look at the yellow pages in any telephone book in any Canadian city, and compare the number of private employment agencies in business in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Hamilton in 1963 with the number which were in business in 1953 or 1948. If the employment service were doing a good job these private agencies would never get the business they have.
The objectives of a reconstituted national employment service in the labour department should be, first, to maintain a continuous review of Canada's manpower and to develop a long term plan for the effective deployment of the total manpower resources of the country.
I was disturbed tonight when the minister spoke of an extension of the department's role of counting how many people are unemployed and how many jobs are needed. I did not detect in his speech any note of urgency concerning aggressive action on the part of the department in planning for full employment.
Second, the reconstituted national employment service should ensure that everyone who needs employment has access to a job which makes full use of his productive capacity.
I commend to the minister a thought expressed by a man whom nobody in this house
[Mr. Orllkow.j
would consider a flaming radical, the head of a large business organization, the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, Mr. R. M. Fowler. I am told he is also a pretty prominent Liberal, and I wish to read into the record a short paragraph from a statement he made before the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment in 1961:
In the modem Industrial state, there is a responsibility of society to provide work for people who want work. It is no answer to make statistical arguments that the existence of some degree of unemployment makes other economic problems easier to handle-such as, for example, the control of inflation. Nor is it any answer to say that present unemployment afflicts only a minority of Canadians; for that minority it is still a major misfortune. These human losses are also national losses; the goods and services that a man could have produced on a day when he is unemployed are lost forever and the total wealth of the nation is reduced by that amount.
That is an excellent statement. A few years ago it would only have been we woolly minded socialists, who did not believe in private enterprise, who would have made that kind of statement; but Mr. Fowler is a pretty hard minded businessman, and the minister should consider his kind of thinking seriously and get on with the objective of obtaining full employment in Canada, rather than putting up with the 5, 6 or 8 per cent unemployment which we have experienced since about 1956.
Lastly it seems to me the reconstituted national employment service should ensure effective mobility of labour through adequate training programs and travel grants, to encourage real upgrading and reallocation of the labour supply.
To do these tasks the employment branch of the Department of Labour needs to have a staff trained and directed to place top priority on job placement today, as well as making plans to meet the new problems which are being created every day and week by automation and technical innovation. Only last week I read in an Ottawa newspaper that Mr. John Snyder, a former secretary of commerce in the United States, estimated that 40,000 jobs are being lost every week in the United States due to automation. I do not know if we can apply that figure proportionately in Canada, but I do not think it is far out, and we are only beginning to tackle the task of finding jobs.
I hope the minister will not continue to be as satisfied as he seemed to be tonight. The Prime Minister has told us about a few of the goodies which he hopes parliament will pass before Christmas, but when we come back in 1964 I trust the minister will try to do some of the things I have mentioned and, if

he does, the members of this group will support him and see that they are passed through the house.

My first words are to congratulate the minister on his appointment to the office he holds. I think members of the committee will agree that one of the very serious problems which faced Canada during the past few months was one directly involving the Department of Labour. I refer to the problem of the maritime unions on the great lakes, and I am sure all hon. members of the committee would wish to commend the minister for the manner in which he handled that situation.
I have been accused of commending the government on a number of previous occasions for certain actions which it has taken. That does not worry me very much. I also commended the previous government when I thought it deserved it, and when the present government deserves criticism I can assure it that I will be offering that criticism.
Tonight I want to deal with one very important matter, the problem with respect to the manifestation of the division between French and English speaking Canada. A large part of the root of this problem lies in unemployment and in low, or lagging, economic conditions in the province of Quebec. I spent last week end and the previous week end driving through various parts of Quebec trying to pick up local opinion with respect to this division between English and French speaking Canada, and from the conversations I had I am convinced that if we could do something to enhance the economic conditions in Quebec we would move a long way toward solving this division.
I wish to quote from a speech made by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine as reported at page 4374 of Hansard for last Monday, November 4:
-I believe that as far as my own province, the province of Quebec, is concerned, unemployment and the economic situation of its population are probably the main cause responsible for the uneasiness which prevails in the federal-provincial relations and in the relations between French speaking and English speaking Canadians.
On that same date the hon. member for Quebec West had this to say, as found on page 4372 of Hansard:
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wish to mention again to the hon. members that they committed themselves, during the election campaign of last May, to stop unemployment once in power, and in my opinion it is about time that they seriously think that over and introduce adequate legislation in that connection.
1 hope you will forgive me, Mr. Chairman, because I have a number of other quotations I want to read into the record from speeches 28902-5-293
Supply-Labour
in the house by members from Quebec who have stated repeatedly that the unemployment problem is at the root of the division and that they expect the federal government and the parliament of Canada to do something about it. Again, the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine had this to say on May 22 this year as found on page 153 of Hansard:
Well, Mr. Speaker, how can the citizens of the province of Quebec, who consider themselves as full-fledged citizens, who want to be considered as equal partners in Canada, be willing to accept a situation where they are at a financial disadvantage compared to the citizens of Ontario?
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who I am pleased to see is here tonight, had this to say as found on page 328 of Hansard for May 27 last:
Nothing contributes more to frustration and bitterness or loss of confidence in one's country and its social system than long periods of unemployment. The relatively poor economic conditions in Quebec provide a major source of discontent among the working people and farmers in that province.
The hon. member for Lake St. John had this to say, as found on page 328 of Hansard for May 27 last:
I come from Quebec, a province which is most particularly affected by the unemployment which prevails in Canada. Nearly 10 per cent of our labour force are out of work and all the people of my province have their eyes turned toward Ottawa to see what the federal government intends to do, through the provincial governments and especially through the Quebec government, to reduce the number of unemployed.
After having spent a few days in Montreal and one day in the city of Quebec and several days in other parts of the province, I believe there is a genuine frustration among some of our French speaking Canadians who do not have a sufficient command of the English language to aspire to some of the top positions in commerce in Canada today. But I wish to contend that the international language of commerce is English, whether we like it or not. Furthermore, it is not because of anything that English speaking Canadians have done that this has come about. I do not think it is even something that England itself has done in latter years that has brought this about. I think it has come about because of the expansion of American influence in the world, particularly in the world of commerce, for certainly that expansion has been carried out in the English language.
Therefore I implore our colleagues from the province of Quebec to stop blaming the English speaking members of this house for this problem. Even if Quebec were a separate state the people there would still be faced with the international language being English in dealing with all the countries in the north Atlantic region, and in many other places in the world.

Supply-Labour
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I am genuinely interested and concerned in doing something about this problem. The members from the province of Quebec whom I have quoted have stated one after the other that it is the responsibility of the federal government and this parliament to take some action to equalize the situation. So my challenge to these members tonight is to come before parliament with some kind of program that will do the job and at the same time be acceptable to the province of Quebec.
We know, for example, that in past years when the trans-Canada highway program was established it was rejected in its initial stages by the province of Quebec. We know, for example, that when assistance with education, particularly to universities, was offered to all students at any of these institutions all over Canada this was rejected by the province of Quebec.
By Duplessis.

If we turn to more recent history we find that the municipal development and loan fund established at this session of parliament was also partially rejected by the province of Quebec, even though this legislation was supposed to do more than anything else to solve the unemployment problem in Canada.
The province was right, too.

I want to say in fairness that we in this party have asked for years that a municipal development bank be set up and we are still of that opinion. There is a slight difference between the operations of a municipal development bank, such as we have advocated, and the municipal development and loan fund that was actually established. There are provisions for the forgiveness of certain amounts and there are also provisions that the money must be used for certain things.
Taking that into consideration and at the same time taking into consideration the provisions of the Financial Administration Act, which demands that money voted by parliament be accounted for to parliament, the department administering the development and loan fund has got to follow through to see that the money is used for purposes that were authorized by parliament. That part of the legislation is not acceptable to Quebec, if I understand their attitude correctly.
The province of Quebec has contracted out of the Canada pension plan even before it has got under way. It is not under way, and perhaps they saw the light first because in my opinion it was introduced before all of the problems had been anticipated. Its introduction was premature.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I think the province of Quebec has its reasons for refusing to enter into an agreement with the federal government and I think we from the province of Quebec have no lesson to learn from the hon. member.

There is no question of privilege or order or anything else. I would remind the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm that he and I are members of the parliament of Canada and that we should always keep that in mind. I am not here tonight to try to teach a lesson to anybody from Quebec or anywhere else. The fact is, however, that parliament has been under a steady barrage of complaints from members from the province of Quebec that we should do something to relieve the unemployment situation there. As I said, I am willing to support measures that will do this, but I want to know that the province of Quebec is going to accept them. Many of the things that have been done over the years have been rejected out of hand by the province of Quebec on the pretence that they infringed on provincial autonomy.
There are precedents for passing legislation that is of benefit to certain regions in Canada. In this session of parliament, for example, we have passed the Atlantic Development Board Act and have provided a fund of $100 million for the special benefit of that area. I have no objection to passing such legislation, even specifically for the province of Quebec, provided they will make use of it.
I also remind hon. members that back in the 30's a number of such acts were passed by parliament. For example, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was of specific benefit to one area of Canada alone. We appreciated that and it has done a lot of good over the years. Then there is the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which also assisted a certain area. It is no disgrace to any area of Canada that it should happen to be lagging behind some other area economically. It would be a strange situation indeed if one particular province or one particular area would be ahead all the time.
In the past we have passed legislation in this house for the benefit of the prairie region, while in the last few months we have passed legislation for the benefit of the Atlantic region. I have no objection to supporting legislation that will be of benefit to any other area that is economically depressed at this time. As I said, Mr. Chairman, I should like to have some assurance that if we do what we are expected to do and a program is brought in and passed it will be accepted and used for that purpose.

I should like to spend a couple of minutes on the vocational training program. The member who spoke immediately before me said it was not proceeding rapidly enough, and perhaps that is true. It is true if you take into consideration the number of unskilled workers in the country who are unable to obtain jobs. I want to be fair and I would even congratulate the former minister for setting up this program in the first place; but it should be drawn to the attention of the committee that the people at the local administrative level who are trying to make the best use of the vocational training program are breaking new ground all the way. They had no programs or surveys of what was required. They did not have the staff or facilities to get on the with job. We have one of these schools in Medicine Hat and I am glad it is there. About $24 million worth of school building and equipment are ready to be used. But when it comes to programming and finding the needs required to fit programs to train people it becomes a different kind of task. I know a number of members on the school board, particularly the superintendent of public schools, in Medicine Hat in charge of setting up these training programs and educational programs, and it is not easy; but they are moving as fast as they can and it is a matter of trial and error. Quite frankly I congratulate them on the progress they have made to this point. It is not as rapid as it perhaps could be, but this is not because of lack of effort. We have excellent facilities. The school is almost overbuilt and the present facilities cannot be fully used either this year or even in two or three years to come. I think it is rather an unfair criticism therefore to say the program is not going ahead as fast as it should. I have looked at some of these statistics and the provinces of Ontario and Alberta took the greatest advantage of this program. After a while the other provinces will be able to benefit to a large extent from the experience learned in these two provinces.
In closing, I just wanted to draw these few matters to the attention of the committee and hope that in weeks to come, when we hear of unemployment problems in various regions of Canada, we may also hear suggestions from those same areas which will in fact be an acceptable solution to these problems.

In rising to make some brief comments on the estimates I would not only compliment the minister on his appointment but also compliment him on the manner in which he has carried out his heavy responsibilities. Everyone in Canada agrees that no minister of labour was ever faced with more serious problems in so short a time 28902-5-2934
Supply-Labour
as the present minister over the last six months. I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North and to a great extent found myself in agreement with him, when he deplored the lack of a review and systematic amendment of our labour legislation. I agree the time has long since passed when all the labour legislation of our country should have been thoroughly reviewed and changes brought about to bring it up to date in light of changing conditions, both in labour and management, during the last 20 years. The recent trouble with the S.I.U., culminating in the present trusteeship, is an excellent example of the need for changes in our labour legislation. In speaking in the debate at the time the trusteeship was established I had occasion to mention that our legislation should be brought up to date so that other gangster czars of the Hal Banks type would not have the opportunity to come into power in the future. I suggest in that direction it is time we considered seriously the necessity of outlawing the "closed shop" in certain types of industries in order to prevent a would-be union czar from having too much control beyond our democratic processes. There are also many active today in the union movement in Canada who agree that we need some form of review by governmental or other appointed authorities of union welfare plans and finances so that members' interests can be protected. In this regard caution must be shown by this house in amending legislation so that the freedom and independence of our labour movement would be protected.
Nevertheless there is no question that the parliament of Canada by default has given to the courts the job of deciding the course of development of our labour laws during the past 20 years. Owing to the fact that we made no changes in our labour laws to keep them up to date it has been left to the judges to adjudicate upon all types of situations which arise in modern management-labour relations, many of the present situations being of a type not even contemplated at the time when our first labour relations legislation was enacted. I suggest that in many instances there would be a goodly number of Canadians who would disagree with the course the courts of this country have seen fit to follow in this direction.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

No. We need statutory clarification of the right to picket peacefully, and of the legality of secondary boycotts in view of decisions made by the courts, which have not seen fit to follow the rather liberal interpretation of workmen's rights as established

Supply-Labour
in England by the Crofter-Veitch and Thomp-son-Deacon eases. In this country the courts, acting in the absence of the legislators through default of parliament, have seen fit to invent with great imagination and originality a supposedly new tort of conspiracy. We have now reached what I call an unreasonable condition that any strike not wholly in accordance with the law becomes outlawed to the point where it is conspiracy in the eyes of the law, so that in effect strike activity can be restrained and the rights of the workers to collective representation is, in the end result, invariably lost. In other words, under the present status of the law if the union, in carrying out the necessary secret vote before a strike is called, make some technical error and does not comply with the letter of the law, everything happening thereafter becomes an illegal conspiracy making the union subject to injunction, and to be sued for very heavy damages.
These are situations which I suggest were never intended by parliament and which do not exist under the laws of England. I submit that the spirit of the bill of rights and, indeed, in the spirit of the earlier decision of the Aristocratic case in British Columbia in 1951, which decided that workers at all times have the right to free speech and to communicate their side of any dispute regardless of whether they were in the right or in the wrong, has unfortunately not been followed subsequently by our courts. In order to bring our labour laws back in line with developments in this branch of the law, it is high time we had a complete review of the labour legislation of this country.
I intend to be brief, but before sitting down I should like to say I am looking forward to the establishment by this government of a national labour code. I hope and feel it will not be long in coming and it is certainly badly needed. Before concluding I should like to say that we in Canada have been very fortunate in our labour relations inasmuch as we have had in the past, as we have today in the Canadian Labour Congress, a union organization which represents the great majority of the responsible law-abiding progressive unions of the nation.
We are very fortunate in having such an organization which has at all times taken a broadminded approach to the problems of the economy of this nation, an organization which other countries would be proud to have as their central labour organization.
Finally, I would urge that the government make every effort to see to it that an early review of the now outdated labour legislation of this country can take place so that we in Canada can again become leaders in this field.

Mr. Chairman, I had no
intention of taking part in this debate but in view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), I felt it was my duty to protest strongly on behalf of the vast majority of people in my province.
True, the province of Quebec does have 40 per cent of the total number of unemployed in Canada. My province needs its powers of taxation to settle its problems, including unemployment.
Quebec's culture and outlook are different from those of the other provinces, and that is what made confederation possible.
My province is quite willing to co-operate with the other provinces to make Canada stronger and more powerful, as long as the federal government, regardless of which party is in power, respects its wishes. That is how Canada will become a strong and powerful country.
For several years now, the central government has been infringing upon the jurisdiction not only of Quebec but of all provinces. No protests were voiced by some provinces but Quebec was right in speaking out because it is not a province like the others. It has its own characteristics and I think that the various and successive provincial governments opposed joint programs, and I agree fully with their stand. In fact, I hope that at the next federal-provincial conference, the central government will accede to the request of the province of Quebec. Should it fail to do so, it would be responsible for the secession, before long, of French Canada from English Canada.
I wish to emphasize this, because under our constitution certain rights have been recognized to the provinces.
At the time of the war, the federal government infringed upon the rights of the provinces, and it should as far as possible comply with the requests made every year by the province of Quebec, so that the latter could regain control of certain fields and carry out some work projects.
If the federal government were to agree at the next federal-provincial conference to turn over to the province of Quebec, and to other provinces as well-because the province of Quebec is not the only one to want it-* more taxation powers in order to promote education and other economic and cultural endeavours, I am convinced that this would be the best way of solving the unemployment problem, not only in the province of Quebec, but in the other provinces also.
Mr. Chairman, as I said earlier, I did not intend to speak but the hon. member for

Medicine Hat criticized the province of Quebec for refusing to co-operate with the federal government about the pension plan. Well, Quebec needs the money in that reserve fund precisely to meet its own economic needs and thus help check unemployment.
I also wished to protest strongly, and I say it again, against the remarks made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. In fact, the hon. member does not know the province of Quebec well because spending only a few hours there, as he did, is not enough to enable him to know the feelings of the province of Quebec.
In my opinion, the hon. member should instead spend two and even three months there, but even then I would be very much surprised, in view of the mental capacity I find him to have, if he managed to understand the aspirations of the province of Quebec.
The province of Quebec will work for a greater Canada, as long as its rights and privileges are respected.

In the same vein, may I say it is interesting to notice these box scores in the columns of the press on the attendance of members of the House of Commons. I do not know whether it is because I have got to my feet, but I notice there are now five representatives in the press gallery. During most of the evening there have been only two. I hope that box score will be published as well. I may say our proceedings have been well covered by the charming representative of United Press International and by a capable representative of the Canadian Press. But the representatives of the newspapers of Canada who have so much to say about our attendance and our discharge of our duties seem to have taken Friday night off. I hope they will report this. I hope, at least, it will be transmitted in the dispatches of the Canadian Press and United Press International.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
As the members of the committee know, Canada holds a seat on the governing body of the International Labour Organization by virtue of the fact that we are recognized as one of the ten most industrialized nations of the world. We are also aware that the nature of our economy has changed across the years, particularly in recent decades. We have become a highly industrialized nation and, in all probability, this trend will increase. I mention this in order to support the point of view expressed earlier this evening by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North to the effect that the Department of Labour should become much more than just a set of referees in industrial disputes; it should become a department which takes a positive lead in the promotion of full employment, in the promotion of education, in the promotion of training and retraining, and in bringing forward legislation which will enhance the position of those who work in Canadian industry.
This is why we feel full attention should be given to these estimates. This is why we had hoped that the able and scholarly Minister of Labour, who is capable of giving an excellent treatise on these matters might have given us a little more substance in the remarks he made tonight. I know he indicated his willingness to answer questions after other hon. members have spoken. I hope that having listened to whatever speeches are made tonight he will give the speech he should have given at the start. I hope he will have noted not only the remarks which were made on this side of the house but the appeal addressed to him by the younger member for Halifax-at least, I think he is the younger one-for action on the question of a national labour code. We have labour legislation on the books of this country. We have had a trade unions act for a long time. We have had other bits of labour legislation for many years. But it was not until 1948 that we got anything comprehensive in terms of federal labour legislation. I refer to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which we did not get until 1948. We did not get the Unemployment Insurance Act until 1940. These two pieces of legislation came in those years, despite the fact that in 1919 the party which is now in power pledged itself to go to the limit with respect to the

Supply-Labour
items that were incorporated in the 1919 peace treaty and set out in the terms under which the International Labour Organization was established.
It not only took all those years to get on the statute books the two main pieces of legislation to which I referred, but since then very little has been done. There have been no significant amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act since 1948. While the Unemployment Insurance Act has been amended a number of times since it was enacted in 1940, it is now due for a thorough overhaul. We have been promised that something will be done in this field, but it looks now as though this cannot be counted on until the next session of parliament.
There is another area, Mr. Chairman, in which labour legislation is required, apart from measures such as the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and the Unemployment Insurance Act. I have in mind what is now generally referred to as a labour code. I was glad to hear other members, particularly the Liberal member for Halifax, talk about the need for a labour code. Sometimes he talked about the need for revising it. The difficulty with the use of that word is that there is no labour code to revise. It is a purely arbitrary exercise to say what items are included in a labour code, what items are included under the heading of industrial relations, and so on. But it does seem to be generally recognized that a labour code ought to include at least these five things: legislation respecting minimum wages; legislation governing maximum hours of work; legislation on a maximum work week; vacations with pay, and statutory holidays with pay.
There are other things, such as the question of a check-off of trade union dues. There is the question of legislation for equal pay for equal work, which we have on the statute books. If I may confine myself to the five items that I said were really the minimum elements of a national labour code, I should like to point out that, so far, only one of them is on our federal statute books, namely legislation for vacations with pay. Even that was not put on the statute books by the Liberals. It was put on the statute books while the Conservatives were in power, despite the fact that as long ago as 1919 the Liberals, in that great convention that selected Mr. King as leader, promised significant legislation in this field.
About once a year I like to get from the library the book that reports the 1919 Liberal convention. It is a very interesting document. As a matter of fact tonight, for the first time,

I found that one of the delegates at that convention in 1919 was the late Mr. F. C. Hamilton of Winnipeg, who was chairman of the board of the church in which I was minister the first time I ran as a political candidate back in the federal election of 1935. Let me say that although he was an active Liberal, and even though he did not agree with my politics, he recognized my right to enter the political field.
