speechtext:
I did not realize that a mere favourable reference to a late friend of mine who happened to be a Liberal was going to produce this exchange and this point of order. I was just inviting members to do as I do once in a while, and read the promises made by the Liberal party in 1919. Amongst other things, of course, they promised measures in the social security field that perhaps are not relevant to the discussion tonight. I will quote them again on another occasion.
However, the Liberals did promise in 1919 that they would adopt the proposals of the International Labour Organization, that we would have a maximum hours per day law and a maximum days per week law. Hon. members would be quite proper in drawing my attention to the fact that I have not mentioned the number of hours that was promised in those days. We have moved from that day to goals that are more advanced, but on the federal statute books there is no law fixing the maximum number of hours or the maximum number of days per week. There is still no minimum wage law and there is still no provision for statutory holidays with pay. In so far as annual vacations with pay are concerned, there is a bill on the statute books but it was put there by a Conservative government when it was last in power. The Liberals, when they were in opposition, agreed with us that this legislation should be improved, but as yet nothing has been done about it.
When the Liberals were over on this side of the house in the last parliament, they were strong in their insistence that there should be a national labour code; that this kind of legislation on minimum wages, maximum hours, a maximum work week, vacations with pay and statutory holidays with pay, should be introduced. They have moved across the way and they still think it should be introduced. The hon. member for Halifax said so tonight. The hon. member for Essex West on May 30 in this session when speaking to one of my bills in this field suggested that this was not the way to do it, bringing in one bill at a time, but that what we should do was to bring in a national labour code. He admitted he could not speak for the government, but he was sure that before long a national labour code would be introduced by the Liberal party.
On that same day the hon. member for Kootenay East, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour, expressed the same
Supply-Labour
sentiment. The way to do this, he suggested, was not by bringing in one piece of legislation at a time but to wait for Liberals to introduce a national labour code. On May 21 the Prime Minister was asked about one of these items, namely minimum wage legislation. He replied on that day that it would be introduced as soon as possible. I asked the present Minister of Labour on June 5 of this year when these items for a labour code which had been promised by the Liberals in the last election campaign were going to be introduced and he assured me, as can be found in Hansard for June 5, page 699, that these matters were under active consideration and would be on the order paper in due course.
Well, Mr. Chairman, there is the order paper; look at it and you will see that not one of these items is on it in the name of the government. There is no indication of a national labour code. The other day when the Prime Minister told us what the business would be for the balance of this session, there was no reference to a national labour code. Even when we look over the promises that the government has made for the next session, this does not seem to be in sight.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is quite fair on my part to refer back to 1919 and to speak in terms of the Liberal party that we have today as the Liberal party that came into power at the next election after that year's Liberal convention and which has continued the traditions of that time. It is a long time to wait, from 1919 to 1963, 44 years, and still not have implemented the things that were promised at that time. For the benefit of the hon. member for Hamilton East, let me read a paragraph from Mr. Mackenzie King's speech at the end of that convention, the convention that adopted these progressive labour planks such as the labour code to which I have just referred. This was his speech which concluded the convention at which he had been elected leader, and was away to his future career. These are Mr. King's words:
If more is needed, that more is to be found in the platform which has been laid down by this convention. That platform, ladies and gentlemen, is the chart on which is plotted the course desired by the people of the country, as expressed through the voice of the Liberals assembled here. So with this chart and this compass, forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, let us press on from this moment, a great, a united, a mighty force, making ever for new liberty, for wider freedom, for greater righteousness in the public affairs of this nation; press on, ever more zealous and united, till we have reached the goal where the principles and policies laid down on this historic occasion will have become-
-and I pause now to emphasize the next two words-
-through legislation-

Supply-Labour
-and the rest of the sentence reads-
-part of the law of our land.
I do not think it is unfair on my part to say to the Liberal party in power today that these many years later we should not still have to be asking, as the hon. member for Halifax was asking tonight, for the Liberals to put into legislation the things they have promised across the decades. I urge upon the minister as strongly as I can to pay heed to what has been said to him from both sides of the house about a national labour code.
Proposals along these lines are before him in terms of private members' public bills that we have placed on the order paper. We are willing that these bills be passed or that their subject matter be referred to committees, or that any other course be taken, provided the government will recognize the importance of a national labour code to the industrialized economy we have now in this country.
I just want to mention one or two other things, and I mention them briefly, because the main part of what I wanted to say I have now presented to the minister. I want to hear from him on this question of a national labour code before this item of the estimates is concluded. I also want to tell him that when we get to the item that deals with the International Labour Organization we would like to hear what the government plans to do by way of ratifying some more of the conventions and recommendations passed by the International Labour Organization.
Canada has been a member of this organization since its inception. Canada has voted for many of the conventions and recommendations passed at the annual conferences of the I.L.O., but we have ratified very few of them. I hope this government will do better than the last Conservative government, and better than the previous Liberal government did in this important field.
I also support the position taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, that the national employment service should be separated from the unemployment insurance commission where it is used, we feel, mainly as a test of employment for the purposes of getting or being denied unemployment insurance. We think it should be brought directly under the Department of Labour and pushed as a major activity of that department.
These are the main things we want to place before the minister tonight, and I express the hope that he will deal with the points raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, and this whole question of a national labour code.
Now that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has slipped behind the curtains and may not raise another point of order, I wish to say I have received a note from

the press gallery from the faithful representative of the Winnipeg Free Press. He was hidden by the post and I did not see him. I am happy to include him among the members of the press gallery present tonight.

Mr. Chairman, we are considering tonight the estimates of a very important department, namely labour. In fact, the department is probably the one which is most influential, works the hardest, offers the greatest number of suggestions and carries out the largest number of studies concerning the various solutions which are proposed to the provinces and the whole of Canada.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) receives representations from all sectors of the Canadian economy, be it mining, industry or even agriculture. Day in and day out, he is always besieged by problems. Mention was made tonight of the feeling and the turn of mind prevailing in the province of Quebec regarding its economic situation. It was even asserted that members who represent Quebec ridings, that the people in Quebec, are not satisfied, because it is simply an economic matter if there are in Quebec more unemployed than anywhere in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, since the hon. member for Medicine Hat said earlier that the province of Quebec was turning down any assistance from Ottawa and that the great number of unemployed in our province was due to the turn of mind of the people and the members from Quebec, I say this to him: Ottawa collects $640 million more from the province of Quebec than the province gets from Ottawa; that is the difference between what is collected from and what is given to Quebec-$640 million.
It will be claimed that this amount is used to help either the maritime provinces or some western provinces, especially when we had to subsidize wheat in the west because foreign takers or buyers could not be found, or to subsidize the maritime provinces which are depressed at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, Quebec is not asking Ottawa for preferred treatment. But if Quebec refuses to participate in joint programs, or pension plans, it is because it wants to preserve its sovereignty, its autonomy. Quebec does not want Ottawa to interfere in its affairs. Quebec is only asking Ottawa to leave to Quebec what belongs to Quebec. I think the province of Quebec could very easily find ways to use those $640 million which are taken from it.
The situation of Quebec is different from that of Alberta or British Columbia. At the

present time, British Columbia is asking Ottawa to ratify a treaty between British Columbia and the United States regarding the development of the Columbia river. You do not hear Quebec complaining about that request by British Columbia.
You do not hear either the province of Quebec complaining because Alberta deals directly with the United States about the operation of its oil wells. Certainly not.
The province of Quebec is not complaining either because industrialized Ontario sells directly to the United States or even to other foreign countries. Quebec is far from asking for preferred treatment. Quebec only wants to be respected.
With respect to the hon. member from Alberta, that is the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), who asserts that the outlook, the turn of mind of the hon. members coming from the province of Quebec is not right, that is probably the cause of separatism and independentism in that province. Well, Mr. Chairman, I say that the economic question is of prime importance in our province, just as it is in the other provinces, as well as in every part of the country.
The Minister of Labour, whose estimates are now before us, is well aware of that. We received the day before yesterday a telegram from the Lauzon shipyards' workers union, signed by Rene Barras, which reads as follows:
We protest against the indecision of the government with respect to Canadian shipyards. Some time ago, the government cancelled its program for the building of eight frigates and now it informs us through the press, of the purchase by Canada of three English submarines at a cost of $30 million. These workers would like to know the future policy of the government. Does the government advocate the disappearance of Canadian shipyards, or what?
I suggest to the Minister of Labour that the situation at Lauzon is getting worse, that there is an ever-increasing number of unemployed. These are economic conditions caused by the policy of this government which, instead of providing work for our unemployed by having them build ships, frigates, prefers to purchase them from foreign countries.
We are in favour of buying those things from other countries when it is necessary to do so, but at the present time the situation is urgent in Canada itself, because a large number of workers are having a very hard time.
Mr. Chairman, it has been claimed that the province of Quebec has no solution to offer. But we do have solutions. We are asking the federal government to respect provincial autonomy. We are asking the federal government to give back to the province of Quebec what belongs to her.
Supply-Labour
That telegram proves that a shipbuilding program cannot be carried out in the western agricultural provinces, in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, because they lack the required shipyards. But Quebec and Ontario have them. So why not give the benefits, the priority, to our own Canadian workers?
I give my utmost support to the maritime workers' union which is asking the government for shipbuilding projects, for new contracts which will enable our workers to earn an honest and decent living in their country, in their province and, in this case, in the province of Quebec.
We do have solutions. We have one which has been put forth by the province of Quebec. Quebec has offered a solution to the federal government, that of handing back to Quebec what belongs to her, of handing back to Ontario what belongs to Ontario and of handing back to the other provinces what belongs to each one of them.
Instead of centralizing, let us decentralize and respect provincial autonomy. This is what we are asking, not for one province but for all of them. How can a member from Quebec or elsewhere agree to any other solutions?
The pension plan suggested by the government might very well be applied provincially and by the province itself.
The provinces do not need Ottawa to set up joint programs. Why resort to Ottawa in order to pay an increasing number of bureaucrats and prevent the provinces from enjoying complete autonomy, when they all have an efficient administrative set-up and machinery?
Why not give to the provinces the financial means to look after the decentralization of planning, the development of their natural resources and of the industrial potential now available in Canada? This is the situation prevailing in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada. Quebec is no exception, and it is only a question of Ottawa recognizing the fair demands of the province of Quebec, as well as those of the other provinces.
Mr. Chairman, economic conditions now prevailing in Canada call for the immediate attention of the Minister of Labour. The minister knows that the solutions we are suggesting are practical, applicable and readily workable.
Instead of racking and cudgeling its brains to find new schemes to take from the provinces what little is left to them, why does the government not use the available means, that is the Bank of Canada?
We say over and over again, why should the policy which we are advocating not be applied? It is a possible solution. Why not

Supply-Labour
use the Bank of Canada, in order to develop our natural resources and thus assist the provinces, school boards, municipalities, public bodies in the public administration? This is what the Canadian people are expecting from us, and the government is now trying to meddle in all fields of private enterprise to lower the human being, private enterprise and private efforts. For what purpose? For the benefit of a financial system which has shown its inefficiency.
In fact, was it not the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Towers, who stated in 1939 that the only restriction to the credit required to wage war was the availability of manpower and materials? Credit was available inasmuch as manpower and materials were available. Since we have from 400,000 to 500,000 unemployed-registered and unregistered, listed and unlisted but unemployed just the same-and since between one and two million people suffer from the present economic situation, why not apply the same principle as in wartime?
Mr. Chairman, why not apply in peacetime, in 1963, the same policy as we applied in wartime to put Canada on a war footing?
Why not set Canada on a peace footing, on an economic development footing?
We have the unemployed, we have the manpower and the brains, in fact we have everything we need except the credit which the government refuses to make available when it comes to take advantage of our industrial potential.
Social Credit has a solution which is not based on division. Saying that Quebec does nothing but beg from Ottawa, that it refuses to co-operate with Ottawa and to accept its conditions, does not help in the search for a solution.
Man does not live on bread alone. There is also the mind, the morals, the supernatural, the liberties. The freedom of man is as important as the food he can consume. This freedom we seek for individuals, we seek it not only for the province of Quebec, but also for all the provinces of Canada, without exception. What we are after is not dissension, but unity, a sort of unity based on an economic system which will ensure the development and emancipation of the provinces, and that of the human person in all the provinces.
Then, the Minister of Labour, the officials of his department and all of us will be happy to go before the electorate and tell them: While we were sitting in Ottawa, we passed legislation to put finance at the disposal of the human person, instead of putting the latter at the disposal of the former, as has been the case so far.

Before the hon. member takes his seat may I ask a question? So far as the Canada pension plan is concerned, Quebec has suggested it will be able to handle this matter itself, which I think is probably true. However, the result will probably be that the other provinces of Canada will not have a national pension program. What answer is the hon. member going to give to people living in his riding, but who work in my riding in another province and who will not be able to obtain a pension based on the work they do, whereas if we had a Canada pension plan the border between our ridings, being a provincial border, would be of no consequence?
Any province in Canada can do exactly the same as the province of Quebec.
It would be too slow.

If it is too slow they should move faster. If the province of Ontario wants its own plan, it is up to the province of Ontario, just as it is up to us in the province of Quebec to have our own plan. There is no objection. On a national scale there is no objection from the province of Quebec to meeting with all the other provinces to work out a mutual national plan that could be accepted by all the provinces, but without the intrusion and control of the federal authorities in the matter. If Ottawa can help, all right; but if Ottawa cannot help, then the province of Quebec can look after itself just as Ontario can, and the hon. member's riding also.

Mr. Chairman, although education is constitutionally a primary responsibility of the provinces in Canada, the simple fact is that at least 20 different federal departments or agencies are involved in the expenditure of money on some type of educational program. The departments that are most affected by this common trend toward federal participation in the federal field are national defence, citizenship and immigration, northern affairs and national resources and labour, as emphasized by the minister this evening and by his immediate predecessor.
This condition of federal participation is the result of the needs of our northern people and of our native population, of the members of the armed forces and their families, and of the unemployed, the handicapped, penitentiary inmates and other special groups. But it is due even more to a growing conviction that a modern democracy must view education as a basic human right and that survival depends upon the maximum development of every individual within the country.

Accordingly, Ottawa has become engaged in a wide variety of educational projects including subsidies, grants, scholarships, living allowances, etc. In addition, 84,000 children and 3,500 teachers attend federally operated schools. This federal activity accounts for 10 per cent of all public money spent on education in Canada.
It is significant that the Glassco commission refers to the administration of this varied program as "fragmentation" and emphasizes the fact that no machinery of any kind exists to co-ordinate these numerous educational activities at the federal level. The government should consider establishing, in co-operation with the provinces of course, a federal office of education or a secretariat to perform the following services:
1.	To supervise the educational activities of more than 80,000 students at present attending federally operated schools at a cost in excess of $50 million annually.
2.	To administer a program, in co-operation with industry, of research and retraining of workers required to meet the demands of automation.
3.	To encourage and publicize the comprehensive programs of adult education at present offered by extension departments of universities across this country.
4.	To act as a clearing house for matching grants and other contributions paid to the provinces for university construction, vocational schools, student loans, scholarships, special courses for new Canadians, handicapped children, apprentices, unemployed, etc.
5.	To provide a medium for the distribution among provinces of information resulting from research studies and experiments conducted at the local level by school and university authorities.
6.	To promote a greater understanding among educators through the exchange of teachers and professors from one province to another.
7.	To encourage the provinces to take steps to facilitate the transfer of students from one part of Canada to another with a minimum of disruption in their programs of study.
8.	To co-ordinate the educational work of the Canada Council, the national research council, the medical research council, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and UNESCO.
Let me repeat that these educational services are being performed now, when they are being performed at all, in a fragmentary and hit-or-miss fashion. I suggest it is time that serious thought was given to setting up a co-ordinating agency of some kind with the approval and support of the departments of education in the ten provinces of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to participate briefly in this debate. First of all I would refer to the ministers of labour who have served successive governments since I first had the privilege of coming to Ottawa in 1953. We have been exceptionally fortunate in the calibre of men occupying this position, who have faced their various problems with a real sense of responsibility and sincerity. They have endeavoured to find solutions to these problems, and in this I include the present minister as well as those who have preceded him.
This has been a very interesting evening. It seems as though hon. members have been engaging in pleasantries, and the atmosphere seemed quite congenial until the sudden outburst from the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm in his reply to some harmless observations of my colleague from Medicine Hat.
With regard to the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference, I sincerely hope that the quiet representations and requests from the province of British Columbia will not go unheeded in the thunder of the demands which will be made on the federal administration from other sources.
Although my remarks tonight will be general, they will contain one or two specific points to which I will call attention. We have dealt with unemployment, and looking back across the years this seems to have been a favourite topic of discussion. However, it is not because various governments have failed to recognize the issue but rather that they have been unable to find a satisfactory solution. When the Liberals were in office the Conservatives lambasted them roundly for their lack of concern, but with a change of government this argument has merely shifted around a little. However, that does not detract from the earnestness with which vari-ious administrations have applied themselves to the task. We have all recognized the existence of this problem, but its very existence in a society such as ours is an indictment of our whole system. The matter of unemployment can only be dealt with effectively at the federal level, and that through a proper attention to monetary and fiscal policies.
Reference was made to the statement made by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine which appears on page 4374 of Hansard as follows:
In my opinion, nobody questions the responsibility of the federal government to ensure full employment. It seems that it has been said a long time ago that full employment is at first a responsibility of the federal government.
We fully recognize the fact that provincial administration and policies have much to do with this problem. However, basically I agree that the major responsibility rests with

Supply-Labour
the federal administration because, as I have said, the conduct and direction of monetary and fiscal policy in the wider sphere is the responsibility of the federal government. It is an indictment of this system when we look around and see the hundreds of thousands of unemployed year after year. It seems we just cannot do anything about it. We keep referring to the increasing number of those employed, but yet face the fact that there is an increasing number entering the labour market each year for whom we are failing to find additional opportunities for employment. This has an effect on the morale of our people, and it is understandable that many of them are driven practically to the point of desperation through their inability to meet the demands of, and provide effectively and adequately for, their families. There is also a loss to society as a whole. There is a host of men and women anxious to engage in productive enterprise and gainful employment who, because of the economic situation, are unable to put their abilities and skills to work, not only in their own interests but in the interests of the nation. We must therefore recognize this problem and apply ourselves diligently to seek a solution thereto.
In a previous debate the Minister of Labour enumerated a variety of measures which the government had put into operation in an endeavour to solve the problem. He spoke about our training program, the winter works program, the winter house building program and others. I believe they are all good, but this does not get down to the basic problem. Until we do this these measures will just be palliatives and will not solve the problem of unemployment from the long term view. I think that the various departments of government rather tend to work against each other in the solution of this problem. A short time ago I gave an illustration where the Minister of Finance introduced certain measures in his budget resolution which we, as well as the people across the country, insisted would be detrimental to labour opportunities. Although there was some relaxation of these particular measures we find they were applied in part and will be further applied in stages as we go along. This has more or less frustrated the activities and plans of the Minister of Labour in his effort to solve the problem.
I wish to refer briefly to the plan to promote employment of workers over 45 years of age. The minister is giving this matter consideration and is urging that older workers be given the opportunity of gainful and productive employment. I suggest it would be a good thing in this regard to clean up our own house first. Someone sent to me a cutting

from the Edmonton Journal of Monday, June 24, 1963, which is an advertisement for a handyman, and then in parenthesis appear the words "camp steward". This advertisement reads:
Required for mine operation in northern Saskatchewan, must essentially have carpentry background, with knowledge of routine mechanical and plumbing maintenance, to service company town-site facilities. Applicants must be single, and between the ages of 30-45, position offers starting salary of $450 per month, five weeks annual leave, plane transportation, group pension and welfare benefits, apply in person to-Eldorado Mining and Refining Ltd.
This company is a crown corporation, and it might be a good thing if the government were to give attention to the matter of giving older workers equal opportunities for employment in these agencies which are part of their responsibility. I suggest that matters such as this be taken under advisement and that something be done to ensure that government agencies or crown corporations themselves will not be guilty of discrimination against those over the age of 45. Certain considerations may enter into this problem, but I do not think they should debar these people from providing for their own needs and the needs of those dependant on them.
Perhaps, this matter I am about to raise does not fall directly under the control of the Minister of Labour, but it is a labour problem. The other day on orders of the day I asked a question about certain conservation regulations which have come into force as a result of which a great many fishermen in my area have been unable to engage in fishing during the past fall. When we come back to the fisheries estimates perhaps I will debate this a little further, in light of the minister's reply. Nevertheless an indication was given some time ago that certain measures would be taken to employ these people and to see they had sufficient work to keep them going. Once again, the department should have a vital interest in promoting labour opportunities for those who are deprived of the opportunity of making a living in the field in which they have been engaged. As far as the items on the order paper in connection with vocational training are concerned, they receive our wholehearted support. They are very important because of the changes which are taking place in our economy and in our society. I read recently that it is possible that one person may have to retrain from one to three times during his lifetime because of the changes which are taking place, so it is tremendously important that this work should proceed and that retraining facilities should be made available to all those who because of economic circumstances, have to move from one type of employment to another.

It is pleasant to see the easy manner in which these estimates are being handled. However, an intervention did take place tonight which highlighted one of the most important issues which has arisen in the labour field. I am referring to the provincial attitude which, I believe, will result in the loss of the Canada pension plan.
When I first came to Ottawa I was aware that in many of the areas under provincial jurisdiction there would never be a pension plan because of the management of certain companies and industries. I worked for the gold mining industry. That industry has probably the most reactionary management group ever assembled in any country at any time. It is certainly hundreds of years behind the times in labour relations. The federal government has not given the proper amount of consideration to the situation in this industry, though it should have done so, because to a large extent the industry comes under the jurisdiction of the central government. It is true that many matters which directly affect the lives and welfare of the employees come under provincial jurisdiction. This industry operates differently from any other. The shareholders who own it seldom live in the gold mining areas; they are dispersed throughout the nation and across the world. They have no connection with gold mining and, often, no connection with any other industry except for the shares they buy and the dividends they clip. This has made the industry difficult to organize and difficult to work in. In these circumstances the workers have looked to the federal government for help in solving at least some of their problems.
In none of the gold mines I know of is there any kind of pension plan. The miners have, accordingly, followed with great interest the suggestions which have been made with regard to pension plans over the past five or six years. I believe a great deal of enthusiasm for the Liberal party was generated by its spokesmen who went across the country campaigning on the basis of a Canada pension plan. Well, if the government had gone about making a mess of things it could not have done a better job than by letting the Minister of National Health and Welfare carry the ball in this field. Not only did she allow the province of Quebec to exercise the provincialism which it finds so very easy to operate when it wishes, but she allowed Ontario to make a stipulation that unless there were changes in the plan Ontario would not be interested, either. As a result tonight, when we are studying the estimates of the Department of Labour, there is no indication before us whether those engaged in the mining industry, the lumber industry and similar industries will be receiving a pension or not.
Supply-Labour
I was interested in the two provincial statements which were made tonight, because in my opinion they are so unrealistic. I believe the border between one province and another would be a much more physical thing than it is if, say, unemployment insurance benefits were paid on a provincial basis. I am certain there would be as many conditions and stipulations attached to the receipt of unemployment insurance as there are now to the other segments of the labour code administered provincially. There would be no uniformity and no opportunity for workers to travel readily from one province to another. I think it is unrealistic to suggest that the province of Quebec could go it alone, as the hon. member for Villeneuve has indicated it could. It might be his statement is true, as far as it goes. But Quebec only came into its own, industrially, within the last 15 years and there was a long period during which the people of Ontario and other provinces provided many benefits for Quebec which that province was not capable of providing for itself.
I doubt very much if it would be financially possible for the federal government to bring in a Canada pension plan if the provinces of Ontario and Quebec did not participate. I am almost certain it could not be done by the other provinces. We hear people speaking of co-operative federalism, the theory by which the provinces will get together and tell the federal government how far it will be allowed to go. I think this should also be the attitude of the federal government. They should say this. They cannot afford to allow the Minister of National Health and Welfare to go around the country peddling the idea of a plan. Let us call the provinces together immediately, and let the Minister of Labour see what co-operation he can get for a national labour pension plan placed under the Department of Labour, where it rightly belongs.
We have nothing to brag about in Canada with regard to the Department of Labour. I agree that the present minister has done an excellent job since he took office. I agree that the former minister also did well. I will agree that the officials are probably, in the main, better than the officials of some of the other departments which I shall not mention. But I still do not think there is anything to crow about. Our Department of Labour has many shortcomings. Let me give the committee an example. A young fellow who lived in a bunk-house at Frobisher Bay got into an argument one night with some of his friends about whether the boss of his construction company should pay annual vacation pay. He wrote a short letter to me indicating that this was a simple problem, one which I would probably find no difficulty in answering quickly. Well,

Supply-Labour
I consulted the deputy minister of labour. He did not have the faintest idea. He referred me to Mr. Wilson who had an idea, because he had made up his mind. He had decided these things many times in the past. He makes up his mind and reaches a conclusion, not because the law is there but because he makes the decisions. That is the way in which it is decided. Well, I did not agree with him. I went to the Northwest Territories council and asked them. The chairman did not know whether this applied in the Northwest Territories or not, though the act says it does. He said he would have to ask his lawyer. I telephoned the lawyer. He said he had not been counsel to that body for over a year. He did not know, but he believed the opinion I had received from the other officials was not correct. We then checked with the Department of Public Works because they were the ones who had the contracts. I found it all hinged upon one simple fact-whether or not the government had declared the contract to be in the interest of Canada, or for the good of Canada.
Unless parliament has declared the contract to be in the interest of Canada there is no right to this holiday pay. One might think that since parliament has, presumably, voted money for the project it would automatically be considered as being in the interest of Canada, but apparently that is not the case. A particular little official has to decide that it is in that category. So, after going through four or five departments I had scarcely any more information than when I began. However, the Department of Public Works intends to be specific next time. Next time they sign a contract, the contract will specify that vacation pay must be paid. We will get around the problem by specifying it in the tender. However, it seems to me if we are going to brag about our Department of Labour we should at least make sure that it does the things we have already decided, as members of parliament, we want to do. Vacations with pay should be granted to the people who come under federal jurisdiction. Let us make this provision apply to contractors in the Northwest Territories.
It is a very remarkable thing that the same young gentleman writes me he is now at home because he has a broken leg. He came out of Frobisher with this broken leg, and he was not getting any money. Where do you think we found the money was coming from? It was coming from a trust company in Montreal and not from a compensation board in Quebec, which is the province adjacent to that area in the Northwest Territories. The payment was coming from a trust company simply because some other arrangement had been made. We cannot take much credit for laws like this.

It has been suggested tonight that we should develop a national labour code. I think I can give a warning now that we are going to try to do this when the new territories are set up. We will hold up that bill until we are satisfied with the labour legislation that will be applicable in the new territories. If we are going to set up a new province, let us set up model legislation for the various departments over which the federal government has jurisdiction. Let us not put in some haywire set-up such as we now have which does not apply to those under federal jurisdiction and is completely discriminatory. You almost need a Philadelphia lawyer to find out what it does mean.
We have computers at North Bay now, so perhaps we could use those facilities in order to develop the type of legislation we need. I think a much easier way would be to write in black and white the various provisions we need, so that this federal government would be able to say it is leading the way. Certainly there are members on the liberal side of the house who are familiar with some of the major problems in the labour field. Surely they will have enough gumption to help us develop a labour code of which we can be proud. Let us apply it to the area in which the federal government is responsible.
I am only guessing, but I would think that the federal labour department is probably the third largest such department in the dominion. It would probably follow behind the departments of labour in Ontario and Quebec. It would not be a bad idea, therefore, if the other provinces that were developing new legislation could look at the federal department and say: This program appears to be working on the federal scene, so we are willing to accept it as a minimum in our province. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that about 10 per cent of the working force comes under the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Labour. I think we would find very few of them would be hurt by a minimum wage of $1.25 per hour. I do not imagine anybody would get a wage increase at that level, unless it might be the char staff of the House of Commons or other people in that category. I would think that the eight or nine statutory holidays we would suggest as a minimum for the labour code would be holidays for which the majority of people under federal jurisdiction would be paid. I would think the compensation laws and regulations probably are not worse in the federal field at the moment than the minimum standards we would be able to establish, but they are better than those in most of the provinces.
I think the same situation would apply in nearly all fields that the federal labour code would cover. It would provide the provinces

with an opportunity to upgrade their legislation and in many cases establish unity that is now sadly lacking in much of this legislation.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is not going to be too proud of the federal Department of Labour until he can come before the house and say that he and his representatives have been willing to endorse the labour convention adopted in Geneva. We, in Canada, have adopted less of this labour convention than many of the newly emerging nations in Africa. I think it is time the Canadian public demanded of the federal Department of Labour that they give support to these labour conventions. In many cases it is only because the general public is not aware of the fact Canada has not endorsed them that has allowed the government to continue ignoring many of these conventions.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North mentioned many of the problems we have in organizing and establishing union-management relationships. Many of these problems stem from the fact that we have not endorsed and do not support many of the labour conventions that have been endorsed in other parts of the world. These are some of the things to which I think we should give consideration. The hon. member for Halifax mentioned a national labour code, and this has been referred to by the Liberal party since 1919. We have come a long way since that time and yet things that were suggested in 1919 have not been put into legislative effect. I suggest there are many other things that would bring the labour code up to date and give the federal Department of Labour a position of leadership to which the provincial authorities would give consideration.
There are other problems with which we should concern ourselves. I believe one of them is the lack of intervention by the federal Department of Labour in the many contracts that are signed by this government. Many of these contracts are yellow-dog contracts. They are contracts that are a disgrace to this country and a disgrace to democracy. There are contracts that are signed between unions and companies when there are no employees at all. Contracts are being signed years before they are even going to be ratified. I believe this is something to which no government should be willing to lend its support and should not in any way endorse. On many occasions we have raised specific cases of this nature.
I am sure there are many members who have raised specific cases in relation to the building of the trans-Canada pipe line, because it was one of the worst offenders in many of these labour relations fields. The
Supply-Labour
same situation has applied to all gas line construction in every area where secondary lines are being established. You will find contracts being agreed to before there are any employees of the contractor. This system has worked fairly well for the unions and fairly well for the companies, but damned poorly for the employees whom both of them were supposed to be protecting. 1 think the government should give some consideration to this matter. The one example I cited in the Northwest Territories illustrates the reason I believe the federal government should always supervise the contracts that are being let in those areas in which the federal government has jurisdiction, in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon. Certainly, it would appear to me that when the Department of Public Works signs a contract with a contractor which does not contain the minimum requirements of federal labour laws, that is not in keeping with the spirit or intention of the labour provisions of the government itself. This is something to which the government should give its attention.
There are many things, Mr. Chairman, I am sure that we could say about the Department of Labour that would be good as well as bad. I am sure the minister will hear the good things from other members. There are some faults in the department that should be corrected. I am sure that as they are drawn to the minister's attention they will be corrected. I would strongly urge him, when he replies, to give us an indication of whether or not he is willing to fulfil this pledge that has been made all across the country to establish a national labour code which would result in the improvement of the standards in all the provinces. If he does this, I am sure it will add to the stature of the Department of Labour and the responsibilities they have.
I feel the minister should be congratulated upon what he did in connection with the recent labour dispute which resulted in the establishment of a trusteeship. Although I am not in agreement with what he did, I think he handled the matter very well. I think he made a good choice in the trustees. The minister should be given credit for the manner in which he has handled this matter, and for the fact he is now willing to have the trusteeship report periodically to parliament. I would only caution him that he is going to have a great deal of difficulty in the future every time there is a problem of national importance. I presume the next problem will be in connection with the railway workers. As soon as there is a problem there will be a huge outcry from the public demanding trusteeship as a solution, in each case where the national economy is affected. This is

Supply-Labour
going to be hard to do and I am sure the minister will give his attention to the matter.
In closing I would like the minister to keep in mind that his department has been very neglected in the past, in relation to the number of people it serves. In the main the people it serves are highly paid workers in government services across the nation. They enjoy better wages and higher standards than many other people, and if the minister will give the leadership that he is capable of giving, then this can become a much more important department of the federal government.

I will detain the committee for only a few minutes, but I cannot resist saying a few words as an old, unrepentant socialist, as a socialist who realizes our economy is controlled by the power elite who own the commanding segments of our economy, as they do in the United States, in Great Britain and in a large part of Europe. However, regardless of this unfortunate situation, I wish to congratulate the minister on his appointment and we all wish him well in all he undertakes to modify the ill effects of the system under which we live. I know he is well intentioned, as are most of the members of the house. All of us want to do something to improve the situation under which we live, by pecking away at it slowly from day to day.
I am one who recognizes that under a capitalist democracy it is parliament's role to do what it can to bind up the casualties of capitalism by labour legislation and by unemployment insurance, which in reality is an insurance against revolution. If we did not have unemployment insurance we would have unemployed workers marching down the streets of every city in the country. We all want to do the best we can with social legislation, and so on; but regardless of this, here we are living in this prosperous country, rich in natural resources, and we have hundreds of thousands of Canadians unemployed. Why? They are unemployed because parliament does not control the economy of the country. That economy is controlled by the power elite I first spoke of, whose first concern is the profits of their corporations and not the welfare of the Canadian people or their responsibility to them as a whole.
I give due credit to the minority who do something to consider the communities in which they live, and for the employees whom they employ. However I want to illustrate this situation briefly because it sticks in my gizzard when I think of it.
The other evening I mentioned a mine in British Columbia, the Reeves MacDonald mining company which is a subsidiary of a United

States corporation. The minister's parliamentary secretary knows all about it and I am sure he is sympathetic to the plight of the unemployed miners. Here is a company which refuses to pay its workers the going wage in the district, workers who have the moral support of all communities in the Kootenay area. This company, which made large profits and transferred them to the major holding in the United States, although it has this large Canadian natural resource, refuses to do the right thing by its employees.
Then there is the Falconbridge mining company which has done very well out of Canada and which has very valuable property in it. But because of automation and changing smelting methods it has laid off hundreds of men, and it does not consult the government of Canada to see what it can do for their benefit. However I am sure the minister will do all he can to modify the ill effects of this type of lay-off.
Then we have International Nickel, which has disclosed its intention to lay off about 2,000 workers, at a time while we in this house are trying to do what we can about the unemployment situation. I say without any hesitation that these large corporations are not accepting their responsibilities to the Canadian people and to parliament.
We have large coal resources in Alberta and British Columbia, and we have this manpower idle. I am not saying they can all be coal miners, but what are we doing? We are inviting capital from Japan to develop our coal mines.
Our farmers on the prairies have prospered in recent times, but we cannot pat ourselves on the back on that account. They are prosperous because of the needs of the people of China, the Soviet union and various other countries.
I want to emphasize the fact, and I do not think it can be satisfactorily denied, that powers beyond the control of this parliament actually dictate the direction of the economy, who shall work and who shall be unemployed. All we in parliament can do is bind up the wounds caused by the defects of the system under which we live. I say this without any fear of contradiction, and recognizing all that has been done by parliament to remedy the situation in, shall I say, a tidbit approach, which is the only approach it can take under these circumstances unless it is willing to face the situation head on and challenge these corporations.
Unemployment for thousands will continue as one of the effects of the system under which we live, periodic large scale unemployment, poverty for many people in our country,

low standards of living conditions, and insecurity for many people until parliament is willing to take action to own or control the major sections of our economy. When I say "control" that does not mean we are going to interfere with the day to day operations of corporations, but rather make them accept some responsibility as a result of their control of natural resources which have been granted to them by federal and provincial governments.
In wartime we can mobilize all our labour, create prosperity and do anything we wish to undertake that is physically possible. But in peacetime we sit here doing the best we can, improving this piece of legislation and that piece of legislation, and yet not really doing anything to solve the problem over a long term basis. In 1945, during the last world war loan, we raised over $2 billion in Canada.
I suggest we have got to meet this challenge head on in the not too distant future if we are to maintain democracy in this country and give the Canadian people the prosperity and security to which they are entitled. Parliament can meet these needs at the present time if it is willing to do that, if it is willing to challenge the power of these people who will not accept their responsibility, if it is willing to employ the capital resources of the country and say profits will not come first, but rather the welfare of the Canadian people. That is all I have to say, but I could not resist these few remarks.

I will not delay the minister too long from making his final comments, but there are a few things which have to be said when we are discussing this problem of unemployment. I should say, perhaps in contradistinction to my distinguished colleague from Kootenay West, I feel I am not so much an unrepentant socialist as an analytical socialist, and it is because I am an analytical socialist I feel some things have to be said in the context of this debate on unemployment.
I always have the feeling when we discuss unemployment that we are dealing in unrealities, or that we are trying to fit facts into a framework that no longer exists. I have much the same feeling when we discuss defence matters, that we seem so foolishly to be attempting to devise a policy for defence that is fitted to a set of circumstances that dissolve before our eyes.
I would like to put on the record one or two quotations from a document produced by a very responsible organization, the fund for the republic research organization in the United States, under the presidency of Dr. Robert M. Hutchins, president emeritus of Chicago university. They produce what they call occasional papers and they have issued
Supply-Labour
one quite recently called, "Consumers of Abundance" which is very apropos of our debate tonight:
The advance of science has for many years been undermining the two pillars of our economy- property and work. Each at length has fallen from its place. Property is no longer the primary source of economic power, and ownership no longer establishes the significant, functioning connection between people and the things they consume... Public understanding must eventually overtake this transformation in the relationship of modern man to his physical environment. Fundamental changes in the social order-in man's relationship to man- are therefore in prospect and are already in process... Full employment, for example, now seems to be not only an unattainable but an outmoded objective of economic policy. What takes the place of wages in a workless society? If such a question must be asked, then others follow. Does profit remain a useful standard of accounting in a propertyless society? But these questions are not only too big; they are premature. Before they can even be asked, the scientific revolution that occasions them must be more closely examined.
Then the paper proceeds to examine some features of the scientific revolution. There is one very interesting report concerning the Middle East with regard to which they say:
Obviously, the purpose in designing the automatic petroleum refinery is not to replace the one or two human operators who still remain on the payroll. This was the naive idea of a Middle Eastern petroleum prince for whom an American oil company was building a refinery not long ago. Out of consideration for the underemployed fellaheen who were to squat in the sand outside the refinery fence, he asked whether jobs might not be created by disengaging the robots from the valves. The engineers took him seriously enough to re-examine the entire control system. They had to conclude that no team of human beings could be trained and co-ordinated to do its work.
Then they have some interesting figures.
In the last 10 years, however, as the index of manufacturing output has climbed from 75 to 110, the number of production workers has hovered around 12 million. It is evident that the number is now due to decline. In the electrical industry, for example, production employment shrank by 10 per cent in the six year period from 1953 to 1959; during that same period production in this industry increased by 20 per cent.
Then they have this to say:
In the long run, larger questions must be asked and answered. If a fraction of the labour force is capable of supplying an abundance of everything the population needs and wants, then why should the rest of the population have to work for a living? Preposterous alternatives come forward: give away programs on television suggest that television might be employed to give the abundance away instead of trying to sell it. If production cannot be maintained at a profit under such circumstances, then why should a profit be made? Some other standard of accounting might serve even better to reduce waste and inefficiency.
Then they also say:
The nation's principal economic problem has become that of certifying its citizens as consumers of the abundance available to sustain them in tasks worthy of their time. What disturbs the scarcity economist, of course, is that such certification is likely to be provided by the public payroll. It

Supply-Labour
must be recognized, however, that these activities- along with urban rapid transit, the enhancement and conservation of natural resources, public works, the best kind of medicine, the operation of museums and so on-have never been or can no longer be conducted at a profit. Most of these activities and institutions are now short-changed. With abundance to support the expanding portion of the population engaged in them, we may anticipate that they will assume a higher priority in our civilization.
Then they go on to say:
A really adequate program of assistance to the underdeveloped countries might engage large numbers of disemployed factory workers in teaching their skills to people now entering on their industrial revolution. For some time to come, we can be sure, the real work that remains to be done in the world will stave off the spectre of universal leisure.
But I would point out that in order to do so there will have to be what some of us have been advocating in season and out of season for a very long time, that the productive capacities of our society must be placed at the disposal of such work. It will be impossible, for instance for Canada or any other industrialized country to play a significant part in this work of developing the undeveloped areas of the world unless the surplusses which accrue from our industrial society are made available for that work.
That will require a vast overhaul of our entire fiscal system. It will entail a vast overhaul of our whole system of private ownership. It will necessitate enormous public expenditures both directly within our country and in the shape of long term credits to these areas.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that until the government, either now or in the very near future, faces this problem it will be wasting its time and destroying the hopes of the Canadian people if it produces again and again these ideas that in some way or another we can solve the problem of unemployment in a world which has a decreasing demand for human labour and an increasing capacity for producing material goods. These are the problems we should be facing now, rather than introducing gimmicks to try to put one or two men to work here and keep them at work a little longer or retrain them in the hope that the job for which we retrain them will not disappear before they come on the labour market. Let us reorganize our economy and really solve this problem of production and distribution in a modern industrial society.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will not take very much time in replying briefly to the comments which have been made by hon. members. First, I wish to thank all members who took part in the debate and who were kind enough to extend their good wishes to me and to the Department of Labour, and also to those members who pointed out to

me and the department ways in which the service of the Department of Labour could be improved. I want to assure members of the committee that each of the suggestions put forward tonight will be given the most careful consideration in an effort to apply them in the way that has been suggested by hon. members opposite and on this side of the house as well.
I might mention to members of the committee that in the past several months the energies and activities of the Department of Labour have been almost entirely absorbed in problems of industrial relations. I think it is a fact that in this field the Department of Labour carried the heaviest burden it has carried since away back in the war years, at least, according to some of the experienced personnel of the department. I certainly share the views expressed by the hon. member for Ontario and others with respect to the capacity and dedication of the officers of the Department of Labour.
But notwithstanding these other absorbing activities in the field of industrial relations we have been actively aware of and actively concerned with a number of other problems that have been raised by hon. members opposite. The national employment service is a very important service and I do not think its role has been overstressed at all by the discussion this evening. As I indicated on Tuesday, we have taken steps to strengthen the personnel resources of the national employment service to make it more aggressive and more effective in the allocation of manpower in Canada in a systematic way.
The Gill committee recommended that the activities of the national employment service could be strengthened by severing this service entirely from the unemployment insurance commission and placing it under the direction of the Department of Labour, so that the two phases of the manpower problem, the placement phase and the policy phase, could be properly interrelated and integrated to the benefit of both sides of the equation. At present this problem is under very active consideration and I hope that in the near future it will be possible for me to make an announcement indicating that some steps have been taken in this direction in strengthening the further work of the national employment service.
The matter of the labour code has been raised by the hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Timiskaming and others. I certainly share their enthusiasm and interest in a national labour code covering most of the items enumerated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which are also

in my own mind as the principal ingredients of such a national labour code. It is my view that it might be preferable to bring all these items together, if possible, into a single piece of legislation and have it regarded as a code setting a level for employment standards in Canada.
It is true that the national leader of the Liberal party indicated to the people of Canada in the last election campaign that this would be undertaken by a new Liberal government. As far as I am concerned as Minister of Labour, I have not lost my interest or my determination to pursue this particular commitment to a successful conclusion, and the Department of Labour has already undertaken very extensive preparations in the direction of the development of a national labour code. I hope that the words I used in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will be appropriate and valid as time goes on.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: How long does it have to go on?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The words "in due course" are indefinite, but I hope they will not be so indefinite as to test the patience of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre unduly. We are working actively on this matter at the present time. I should like to be able to assure the committee, but I am not in a position to do so, that this problem will be dealt with at once, but it is not being neglected by any means and it is under consideration not only by the Department of Labour but by the government as a whole at the present time.
A number of other matters were raised. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the ratification of I.L.O. conventions. We are presently taking steps to ratify the convention with respect to discrimination in employment in occupations in Canada and are seeking the concurrence of provincial governments to ratify this convention at an early date.
I think these are the main general points raised by hon. members requiring immediate reply. All proposals which have been made with respect to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act will receive consideration in an orderly development of the program to strengthen the efficacy of the Department of Labour in the fields I have enumerated.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I wonder whether the minister would summon up courage and assure us that these things he has talked about will appear before us in the form of legislative proposals not later than next session: amending the Industrial Relations and Disputes
Business of the House
Investigation Act; a national labour code; implementation of whatever is to be taken from the Gill commission report? I could go on, but if he would assure us of those three for the next session he would be a great Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Subject to the approval of a number of other persons directly involved,
I have no hesitation in saying that we will want to take action on the Unemployment Insurance Act and the labour code within the time mentioned by my hon. friend. I would be very rash indeed to give the same kind of assurance with respect to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act because, as at the present time, I have not, nor has my department given the kind of consideration in depth to the proposals put forward to justify my giving an assurance of that kind. However, we will consider these proposals and perhaps at a later date I will be glad to add this particular suggestion to the rather optimistic prospect I have given in connection with the other two.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We are in a very co-operative mood tonight on this side and have not said a word for two and a half hours. Could we continue a little longer and pass this department? I point out the fact that by way of interim supply we have already passed eight out of the 12 months supply for the fiscal year 1963-64. Money has been spent and programs are going forward. There are still another 15 departments to consider before the Christmas recess and we are prepared to sit longer tonight and pass the department. However, if there is not a disposition on the part of the house generally to complete the department I am not sure we would want to sit more than another 10 or 15 minutes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

We are all in a co-operative
mood but we have been in session since eleven o'clock this morning, and many of us started at nine o'clock. Speaking for my friends over here we would be willing to let item 1 carry so that the general discussion will be over, but we feel the other items are important and deserve more consideration. With the passing of item 1 I think we should recognize it is ten thirty.

Business of the House

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: On Tuesday we will have a supply motion. On Wednesday we will take the third reading stage of the Income Tax Act. When that is completed we will consider the resolutions, first, respecting the appointment of a sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping and, second, with respect to vocational training. I am not sure in which order these resolutions will be taken. I regret very much I cannot project the legislation beyond that stage but negotiations will go on on Monday to arrange something.
